name: Beckey Route (Southwest Face)
approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead (FS Trail #314, ~5,400 ft, on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass), follow the maintained, well-graded Blue Lake Trail through forest and open meadow for about 1.7 miles to a small meadow just past a small stream crossing (the last reliable water). Leave the maintained trail here on a climbers' boot path heading left (east), ascending through granite slabs, talus, and heather meadow toward the gully that drops from the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. The path is steep in places with short sections of 3rd-class scrambling. At a fork roughly 200 ft below the notch, stay left to reach the Liberty Bell-Concord Tower notch (~7,300 ft) — about 2 miles and ~2,100 ft of gain total from the car, 1.5-2.5 hours. The approach gully commonly holds snow into late June, so carry an ice axe (and possibly crampons) for an early-season ascent.
descent: This is the standard descent line for most Liberty Bell summit routes, not just the Beckey Route itself. From the summit, downclimb the upper (4th) pitch about 20 ft to the first ledge, then go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60m rope reaches a flatter area; from the bolted anchor there, one double-rope rappel (or two single-rope rappels if only carrying one rope) reaches the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. From the notch, downclimb the loose approach gully back to the climbers' path and the Blue Lake Trail. All anchors are bolted or fixed tree slings — no natural gear or v-thread anchors are needed.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the Beckey Gully approach and at the Liberty Bell–Concord notch
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed granite spires
Snow lingering in the gully and on ledges into early summer
Crowding on summer weekends with parties stacked on the short route
The approach gully is loose and chossy; parties above can dislodge rock onto climbers below, and a documented rockfall/rescue incident occurred here in 2013 -- helmets recommended year-round

waysIn.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep (dry)
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of SR-20, roughly 1 mile west of Washington Pass, at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required and the lot is small enough that it fills on summer weekends.

Walk the maintained Blue Lake Trail for about 1.7 miles. The turnoff is a signed junction — the sign points straight on for Blue Lake and left for Liberty Bell Trail #727, Climbing Access — and it sits just past a small stream in a meadow, with a large cairn beside it. That stream is the last water you can count on.

Trail #727 climbs hard through granite slabs, talus and heather benches toward the gully that drains the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. In the gully itself the loose ground is least bad if you keep to climber's left for the lower two thirds, then cross and hug climber's right for the rest. Where the boot path forks a couple of hundred feet below the notch, take the left branch; the right branch leads on toward Lexington and Concord's south side.
hazards: loose rock and party-induced rockfall in the notch gully — helmets on before entering, and avoid stacking up under other parties
steep 3rd-class steps on the climbers' path when wet
trailhead lot fills early on summer weekends; roadside parking on SR-20 is limited

waysIn.name: Early-season snow gully to the notch
waysIn.season: Highway opening (typically mid-late Apr or early May) through late Jun
waysIn.notes:
The same line as the summer approach, but the upper gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch commonly holds snow into late June and the boot path through the slabs and heather may be buried lower down. Parties carry an ice axe, and crampons if the snow has refrozen overnight.

SR-20 over Washington and Rainy Passes is gated every winter — it typically closes in late November or early December and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early May, with the exact dates set by snowpack and avalanche conditions rather than a calendar. Until the gate opens there is no drive-up access to the Blue Lake Trailhead at all.
hazards: firm or refrozen snow in the gully — a slip runs a long way over rock
moat at the transition from snow to rock at the base of the first pitch
wet-loose and cornice debris in the gully during spring melt
SR-20 gated in winter — no vehicle access to the trailhead until the highway reopens
waysIn.whyThisWay: Spring to late June after the highway opens, when the approach gully is still full of snow and the boot path is buried; carry an ice axe and crampons for the icy morning snow.

name: The Girl Next Door
approach: A couple hundred vertical feet below the top of the Liberty-Concord notch, locate a side gully on climber's left with a large cave; walk partway up, then move right onto a treed ledge to start.
descent: The route rejoins the Beckey Route line near its top; descend via the standard two single-rope rappels off chain/bolted anchors down to the Liberty-Concord notch. In early July the first rappel from the trees just below the summit used almost a full 60 m rope, so tie stopper knots in the ends. In late September the first rappel tree sits down an exposed slab that must be downclimbed, and the second set of chains is on a cliff edge on the south side; trend skier's right for the last rappel.
hazards: Sandy/loose rock on some sections, notably the 'Kitty Litter Pillar' ledge on P2

waysIn.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Beckey gully, stopping a couple of hundred feet below the notch at the side gully with the large cave
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The approach is the standard Beckey line: Blue Lake Trailhead, about 1.5 miles of maintained trail to the meadow and stream crossing, then the climbers' boot path up through slabs, talus and meadow into the Liberty Bell-Concord gully.

Three pitches. The route rejoins the Beckey Route line near its top, so the descent is the standard two single-rope rappels off chain and bolted anchors down to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch.
hazards: A start that is passed by every party heading for the notch
A cave feature shared with a neighbouring route
Rockfall in the main gully, which sits directly above the start
Early-season snow in the approach gully

name: Northwest Face
approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead (5,400 ft, on WA-20 about 1 mi west of Washington Pass), follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail roughly 1.7 miles through forest to a small meadow/clearing below Liberty Bell. Leave the Blue Lake Trail here on the well-beaten climbers' path that splits left just past a small stream crossing, and follow it up through slabs, talus, and heather benches toward Concord Tower. Rather than dropping into the main Beckey/Liberty Bell-Concord gully, the NW Face approach stays on the climbers' trail as it climbs toward Concord as long as it reasonably can, then breaks left onto a short, well-trodden low-5th-class step (no more than about 10 ft of easy 4th/low-5th climbing — if you're doing more than that you've missed the spot) that gains the little-visited NW plateau of Liberty Bell, a bench of larch groves below the northwest face proper. Total gain to the base is on the order of 2,000+ ft over roughly 2-2.5 miles one-way; plan 1.5-2.5 hours. The gully section below the plateau can hold snow into early summer and sheds rockfall as it melts out, so helmet up through the talus and gully approach; the Access Fund/Washington Conservation Corps have done trail work here to reduce loose-rock exposure.
descent: From the west summit, downclimb and scramble to the top of the standard Beckey Route line and descend that way rather than reversing the NW Face. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail. Expect a queue at the rappels in busy weather; parties have reported stacking up several deep.
hazards: Route-finding on the northwest face is less obvious than the Beckey Route and parties have gotten off-route.
Rockfall hazard from the approach gully and climbers above.
Exposed summit; descend before afternoon thunderstorms.

waysIn.name: Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path toward Concord, then the ten-foot step onto the northwest plateau
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft on WA-20 roughly 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail about 1.7 miles through forest to a small meadow below Liberty Bell. This is the opposite trailhead from the hairpin pond pullout used by the east face routes.

Leave the Blue Lake Trail on the well-beaten climbers' path that splits left just past a small stream crossing, and follow it up through slabs, talus and heather benches toward Concord Tower. Roughly 2,000-plus ft of gain over 2-2.5 miles one-way; plan 1.5-2.5 hours. The gully below the plateau can hold snow into early summer and sheds rockfall as it melts, so helmet up through the talus and gully.
hazards: A rockfall-prone approach gully that holds snow into early summer
A ten-foot step that is easy to overshoot, leading parties onto harder ground
Queues at the popular Beckey rappels in busy weather; parties have reported stacking up several deep
One pitch of the descent can run slightly over 60 m, so a single-rope party may have to downclimb a short section
A loose gully downclimb from the notch

name: Overexposure
approach: Overexposure starts right at the top of the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower, so the trailhead-to-base approach is identical to the Beckey Route: Blue Lake Trailhead (FS Trail #314) → 1.7 miles of maintained trail to the small meadow/stream crossing → climbers' boot path through slabs, talus, and meadow to the fork below the notch → stay left to the notch itself at ~7,300 ft (about 2 miles, ~2,100 ft gain, 1.5-2.5 hours). Because the route begins above the notch rather than at it, budget a little extra time and care scrambling up into the initial belay compared to Beckey Route parties, and expect the same early-season snow in the approach gully requiring an axe.
descent: The route’s 2nd pitch tops out at the same bolted anchor system that starts the standard Liberty Bell descent, so most parties either stop there or continue a few hundred feet of 4th/low-5th-class scrambling to the true summit, then descend the standard way. From the summit, downclimb the upper (4th) pitch about 20 ft to the first ledge, then go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60m rope reaches a flatter area; from the bolted anchor there, one double-rope rappel (or two single-rope rappels if only carrying one rope) reaches the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. From the notch, downclimb the loose approach gully back to the climbers' path and the Blue Lake Trail. All anchors are bolted or fixed tree slings — no natural gear or v-thread anchors are needed. Some parties instead rappel back down the Overexposure line itself, a couple of enjoyable rappels on a mix of bolts and gear or tree anchors, directly into the approach couloir where packs were cached, particularly when the main descent line is congested.
hazards: sustained hard face/crack climbing
high exposure
afternoon thunderstorms

waysIn.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Beckey gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then scramble above it
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Identical to the Beckey Route as far as the notch: Blue Lake Trailhead and Forest Trail #314, about 1.5 miles of maintained trail to the small meadow and stream crossing, then the climbers' boot path through slabs, talus and meadow to the fork below the notch, staying left to the notch itself at about 7,300 ft. Roughly 2 miles and 2,100 ft of gain, 1.5-2.5 hours.

Expect the same early-season snow in the approach gully requiring an axe.
hazards: Exposed opening moves off the notch, above the gully
Early-season snow in the approach gully requiring an axe
Rockfall in the approach gully as it melts out
Two notches on the same ridge that are easy to confuse
Congestion at the main descent line, which shares anchors with the Beckey Route

name: Liberty Crack
approach: Liberty Crack climbs the East Face, and its approach does NOT start from the Blue Lake Trailhead — that's the trailhead for the west-side Beckey Route. Instead, drive to the pullout on the north side of SR-20 at the hairpin curve a short distance east of Washington Pass (about 0.3-0.5 mile past the Washington Pass Overlook turnoff). Park there and walk back (west) along the road shoulder to a small pond on the south side of the highway. Skirt the pond's east end and pick up a boot path — cairned but easy to lose in the dark on an alpine start — heading north into the forest. The path climbs steeply through timber for 15-20 minutes before breaking out onto talus/boulder terrain directly beneath the East Face, about an hour from the car. There is no reliable water on this short approach, so fill up before leaving the car. The main hazards are losing the cairned track in the trees pre-dawn and loose talus/scree footing at the base.
descent:
The standard way off is the two-rappel Beckey-side descent, shared with Liberty Crack (Free), Freedom Rider and the Beckey Route. From the bolted alcove near the summit shoulder where the last pitch ends, traverse third-class ledges climber's left to the double-bolt station - the final few metres to it are exposed - and make the first rappel, under 30 m, down toward Beckey Gully. Do not link this into one double-length rappel to the notch: that variation has a poor reputation for jammed ropes. A second rappel of roughly the same length reaches Beckey Gully and the Liberty Bell-Concord Tower notch, and from there you downclimb and hike the scree and boulder gully below the notch - snow-covered or loose and unpleasant depending on the season - to the climbers' trail and the Blue Lake Trail. Manage the ropes carefully on both: the terrain is steep and snags are the common problem here.

Plan the walk back before you start down. Liberty Crack parties park at the East Face pullout on SR-20 rather than at the Blue Lake Trailhead, so this descent puts you down on the far side of the mountain from the car, meaning either a shuttle or roughly a mile back along the highway shoulder. A rappel line down the east face that returns you directly to your packs at the base of the route has been reported - a bolted line of six stations on the right side of the wall, where a single 60 m rope reaches each station but is tight at a couple of them, so parties carry a second rope or plan a short downclimb. The four-rappel line off M&M Ledge is a real descent, but it belongs to Thin Red Line rather than to this route; do not plan on it here.
hazards: Sustained steep climbing high on the east face with serious exposure
The Lithuanian Lip roof and thin crux pitches demand confident hard climbing or clean aid
Afternoon thunderstorms on the fully exposed face
Rockfall onto the lower pitches from parties and the gully above

waysIn.name: East Face from the SR-20 hairpin pullout
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep (dry talus)
waysIn.notes:
This route is on the east side of the mountain and is not approached from the Blue Lake Trailhead. Drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20 a short way east of Washington Pass and park in the turnout there.

Walk back along the road toward the pass until you see the small pond on the south side of the highway. The boot path starts at the pond's east end and goes north into the timber; it is cairned, but the cairns are easy to lose in the dark on a pre-dawn start, so scout the first few minutes in daylight the evening before if you can.

The path climbs steeply through forest and then breaks out onto the talus directly under the East Face. Reported times run from about half an hour to an hour of steep walking. There is no water on this approach — carry it from the car.

One consequence worth planning for: if you continue to the true summit and take the standard notch descent, you come down on the west side of the mountain and will need a shuttle or a road walk back to the hairpin. Some parties instead rappel the East Face to return directly to their packs.
hazards: loose talus and boulders at the base of the wall
cairned forest path is genuinely hard to follow before dawn
no water between the car and the wall
rockfall from parties on the East Face routes above

waysIn.name: Early-season snow and moat at the East Face base
waysIn.season: Late spring / early summer after the highway opens, while snow still covers the talus
waysIn.notes:
Same trailhead and same cairned path from the pond's east end, but early in the season the talus under the wall is buried in snow that firms up hard overnight. Parties have reported chipping steps in icy snow to reach the rock, and finding the snow lying steeply enough that a slip would carry you a long way down the slope.

Carry an axe and traction, and expect to be in boots for the walk in even when the wall itself is dry.
hazards: deep moat between snow and rock at the base of the wall
hard refrozen snow over talus — a slip runs out badly
SR-20 is gated all winter, so this window only opens once the highway reopens (typically mid-late April to early May)
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late spring and early summer, once the highway is open but snow still buries the talus under the wall; the snow firms up icy overnight, so bring an axe and traction.

name: Liberty Crack (Free)
approach: Drive to the hairpin turn on WA-20 just east of Washington Pass and park at the pullout on the curve (this is a different trailhead than the Blue Lake TH used for the SW/NW Face routes). Walk back toward the pass and find the small pond on the south side of the highway; a cairned climbers' path leaves from the pond's east end and switchbacks up through forest for roughly a mile, breaking out into a talus field directly beneath Liberty Bell's East Face. From the base of the talus, traverse left (climber's left) on 3rd/4th-class ledges for about 40 ft to reach the start of the crack system. This approach is short (about an hour) but steep in its upper section, with a bit of loose talus underfoot near the top — no water source along the way, so carry what you need.
descent: Liberty Crack (Free) tops out at the same alcove/bolted anchor used by the original aid line. From there, work along ledges to a double-bolt rap anchor and make two rappels (about 25 m each, 80-100 ft by different accounts) down into the Beckey Gully — the same rap line used by the standard Liberty Crack and Beckey Route descents — landing near a tree anchor in the gully. From there it's a downclimb/walk down the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch and back to the climbers' path. All anchors on this line are bolted (shiny modern bolts plus a tree station); a single 60m rope is adequate for a one-day car-to-car push, though some parties opt to downclimb the sheltered Beckey Route slab unroped instead of rapping the last section.
hazards: Free-climbing variation uses a newer (2017) bolted slab pitch (P3) bypassing the original aid bolt ladder, which has deteriorated badly from decades of aid traffic — condition of all fixed hardware should be visually checked, not assumed.
Crux P2 ("Lithuanian Lip," 5.13b) is thin, technical face/crack climbing reported as having sparse protection through the crux moves — high-consequence lead fall potential.
Same approach gully as the standard/aid Liberty Crack route can retain icy or snow-covered sections into early summer in cold years; traction/axe useful for early-season attempts.

waysIn.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then 40 ft left along the base
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Drive to the hairpin turn on WA-20 just east of Washington Pass and park at the pullout on the curve. This is a different trailhead from the Blue Lake Trailhead used by the southwest and northwest face routes, and confusing the two costs an hour and a mountain.

Walk back toward the pass and find the small pond on the south side of the highway. A cairned climbers' path leaves the pond's east end and switchbacks up through forest for roughly a mile, breaking out into a talus field directly beneath Liberty Bell's East Face. The approach is short, about an hour, but steep in its upper section with loose talus underfoot near the top. No water; carry what you need from the car.
hazards: Loose talus in the upper approach
No water on the approach
A start that is only forty feet from a different route's start
A descent that lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the East Face trailhead
Snow lingering in the base talus into early summer

name: Southeast Slopes Scramble
approach: Park at the Smithbrook Trailhead (elev. ~4,000 ft) on Smithbrook Road (FR 6700), about 3 miles up from Hwy 2. Start on the signed Smithbrook Trail (part of the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness trail system) and climb via nearly 20 short switchbacks, gaining about 650 ft in about a mile to Union Gap on the PCT — Lichtenberg's summit is visible to the south for much of this stretch once the forest opens up. At Union Gap, turn left (south) onto the Pacific Crest Trail and follow it about 2 miles, contouring below Lichtenberg's east flank, to Lake Valhalla (~4,830 ft), passing through a mix of forest and open meadow/heather and crossing Smith Brook along the way (a reliable water source and a good place to filter before leaving the trail). From the north or east shore of Lake Valhalla, leave the PCT and begin the off-trail portion: contour and rising-traverse around the lake toward the peak's south/southwest side, picking through heather benches, boulder fields, and increasingly loose talus. There is no maintained trail above the lake — expect real route-finding, some bushwhacking through scattered subalpine fir, and a few short cliff bands that force minor backtracking; a GPS track or written beta is genuinely useful here. The standard line aims for a prominent gully on the south/southwest side of the summit tower (often snow-filled into early summer — an ice axe and sometimes light traction are worth carrying outside of peak summer), climbed as scree/talus with a bit of low third-class scrambling near the top to gain the final summit block. Total gain from the trailhead is roughly 2,000-2,500 ft over about 9 miles round trip, with 6-7 hours being a typical leisurely round-trip time. On a fine mid-October Saturday the trailhead lot was full soon after 8 am and the overflow parked at wide pullouts a few hundred feet down the road; the Smithbrook trail was very muddy.
descent: Descend by the same line used on the ascent: down-climb the summit gully (loose scree/talus, care needed with footing and for parties below you kicking rock), then reverse the traverse around Lake Valhalla's south/east side back to the Pacific Crest Trail. Pick up the PCT northbound, follow it back over Union Gap, and descend the switchbacked Smithbrook Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble route with no rappelling required and no fixed anchors on the mountain — rope and rappel gear are not standard kit for this line. The main descent hazards are the loose, unstable talus and scree in the summit gully (helmet recommended, stagger the group to avoid rockfall onto climbers below) and the off-trail route-finding back down to Lake Valhalla, especially in flat light, fog, or if descending after a winter/early-season ascent when the gully may still hold snow (in which case an ice axe and caution on firm morning snow are warranted). Refilling water is easiest at Lake Valhalla or the Smith Brook crossing on the PCT before the final trail miles out.
hazards: loose talus
lingering snow
cliff bands/rock outcroppings above Lake Valhalla can cliff out parties climbing directly toward the summit
unmaintained, overgrown boot path along Lake Valhalla's west shore (no maintained trail beyond the PCT)

waysIn.name: Smithbrook Trail and the crest trail to Lake Valhalla
waysIn.season: Snow-free ground roughly July through October; the same slopes are skinned or snowshoed as a separate winter tour. The access road is unplowed in winter and typically melts out by early to mid summer.
waysIn.notes: From the Smithbrook Trailhead on the gravel spur off the highway, climb the signed Smithbrook Trail through nearly twenty short switchbacks to Union Gap, where it meets the crest trail; the summit is in view to the south for much of that stretch once the forest opens. Turn left and follow the crest trail south, contouring below the mountain's east flank through a mix of forest and open heather meadow and crossing Smith Brook, which is a reliable place to filter before leaving the trail. Where the trail bends away from Lake Valhalla, drop off it down a steep dirt path to the water and follow the rocky shoreline round to the lake's south tip.
hazards: No trail beyond the lake outlet; real tread only reappears on the summit ridge
More than one gully on this side of the mountain and only the middle one is the route
The peak visible from the lake is a lower sub-summit; parties have climbed it by mistake onto slick class 4 and 5 ground
Short cliff bands that force backtracking
Loose talus and scree in the gully with rockfall onto anyone below
The gully often holds snow into early summer; firm morning snow
Afternoon thunderstorms on the open ridge

waysIn.name: Crest trail north from Stevens Pass
waysIn.notes: Park in the north lot at Stevens Pass and pick up the crest trail heading north from behind the maintenance buildings. It contours the slopes above Nason Creek and reaches Lake Valhalla from the west, where you leave the trail and work around the lake to the scramble. It is a few miles longer than the Smithbrook start but needs no gravel road, and it is the usual start when Smith Brook road is under snow.
hazards: Long start from Stevens Pass along the crest trail, a few miles longer than the Smithbrook start
No trail beyond the lake: leave the crest trail on arrival and work around the lake to the scramble
Unmaintained, overgrown boot path along the lake's west shore
More than one gully on this side and the true summit is hidden behind a lower sub-summit that parties climb by mistake
Short cliff bands that can cliff out parties climbing directly toward the summit
Loose talus and scree in the gully with rockfall onto anyone below; lingering snow in the gully
Afternoon thunderstorms on the open ridge
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the gravel Smith Brook road is still under snow or closed, since this start needs no spur road, at the price of a few more miles.

name: X Couloir (Southwest Face) / Standard Route
approach: The X Couloir is most directly approached from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38); the less direct alternative starts at Heliotrope Ridge and reaches the southwest face through the Thunder Glacier cirque. Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start hiking/bushwhacking the old decommissioned road around Pt. 4481 toward Rankin Creek — snow travel (often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch) leads past East Rankin Lake (~5,120 ft) and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, near the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. From camp, an alpine start gets the team into the southwest basin and across the bergschrund crux while it's still cold and firm, climbing roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40° snow and a steep serac step in the X Couloir to the 9,085 ft summit. Total approach is on the order of 7 miles and 3,350 ft of gain to the basin camp. Important — access note: FR-38 (Middle Fork Nooksack River Road), damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since 27 July 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on 25 September 2026, and a separate seasonal gate at Wallace Creek (~mile 10) closes the road December 1-June 15 for elk calving; confirm current road status with the Mount Baker Ranger District (Glacier Public Service Center) before a trip, since the drivable road-end — and therefore the length of the approach — varies year to year.
descent: Most parties reverse the ascent line, downclimbing and rappelling the same southwest gully/couloir system (the X Couloir) back down into the southwest basin below the face. This is a real rappelling descent, not a walk-off: the most detailed documented descent (a repeat/'2nd descent' trip report) describes 10 double-rope rappels — 4 off pickets placed by the descending party, 1 off a sling around a rock, and 5 off pre-existing slings left around rock horns lower in the gully. Bring a rope long enough to rappel on doubled strands plus spare cord/webbing for building or backing up anchors, since fixed tat should never be trusted blindly. Anchors are a mix of natural (slung rock horns and blocks) and improvised (snow pickets), not bolted — expect to build some yourself. The exact rappel count is conditions-dependent: earlier-season parties with more continuous snow have gotten down with as few as 3 rappels off deadman/picket anchors and simul-downclimbing between them, while later-season, rockier conditions push the count up toward the 10-rappel figure above; budget for the higher number and extra anchor material. The gully funnels rockfall and is exposed to spindrift/small slides after storms, so descend early and move efficiently through the narrower constrictions. Once off the couloir, re-rope for the bergschrund and any crevassed ground on the way down to the treeline camp, then reverse the approach - down past East Rankin Lake and around Pt. 4481 on the old decommissioned road - back to FR-38. Do not descend north toward Heliotrope Ridge. With a camp in the Rankin Creek basin, going that way puts you on the opposite side of the mountain with a glacier between you and your camp.
hazards: Notoriously loose, rotten volcanic rock
Complex route-finding on the Black Buttes
Crevasse and serac hazard on the approach glaciers
AI3+ crux crossing the first bergschrund on 70-85° snow/ice
Warm-temperature wet-snow instability in late season

waysIn.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
waysIn.season: Roughly Apr-Jun. A spring snow climb; essentially never done in summer, because what makes it climbable is continuous snow rather than the rubble underneath
waysIn.notes:
This is the more direct way to the X Couloir: from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38). The southwest face can also be reached by a less direct line with more glacier travel; do not confuse either with the north-facing Coleman side, which leads to the other route on this mountain.

Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start walking the old decommissioned road around Point 4481 toward Rankin Creek. Snow travel — often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch — leads past East Rankin Lake near 5,120 ft and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, by the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. Roughly seven miles and 3,350 ft of gain to camp.

Access: FR-38, damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since July 27, 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on September 26, 2026, and a separate gate at Wallace Creek near mile 10 closes the road 1 December to 15 June for elk calving. Confirm the drivable road-end with the Mount Baker Ranger District before the trip; the length of the approach varies year to year.
hazards: FR-38 flood damage with no repair timeline, plus an elk-calving gate closed 1 Dec to 15 Jun, so the approach length varies
Bergschrund crossing (AI3+ on 70-85 degree snow and ice) that must be done cold and early
About 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step, all above a long runout
Notoriously loose, rotten volcanic rock; the gully funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
Wet-snow instability and rapid softening on the southwest-facing line as it warms
Descent is a real rappel sequence off pickets and slung horns, not a walk-off
Complex route-finding among the Black Buttes

waysIn.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Thunder Glacier cirque
waysIn.notes: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead and follow the trail toward the old cabin site, then rope up and cross the lower glaciers south into the Thunder Glacier cirque to reach the southwest side of the peak. It is less direct than the Rankin Creek line, with much more glacier travel, but it starts from a paved-to-gravel road that is usually open when the Middle Fork road is not.
hazards: Roped glacier travel across the lower glaciers into the Thunder Glacier cirque, with more glacier travel than the Rankin Creek line
Crevasse and serac hazard on the approach glaciers
Bergschrund crossing (AI3+ on 70-85 degree snow and ice) that must be done cold and early
About 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step above a long runout
Notoriously loose, rotten volcanic rock; the gully funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
Wet-snow instability and rapid softening on the southwest-facing line as it warms
Descent is a real rappel sequence; going back north toward Heliotrope Ridge from a Rankin camp puts a glacier between you and camp
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the Middle Fork Nooksack road is closed or washed out; the Heliotrope road is usually open, but expect far more roped glacier travel.

name: North Slopes
approach: From the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead (~3,500 ft, end of Eightmile Road/FR-7601), follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) about 2.5 miles to the signed fork where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599.1) splits left/south. Continue roughly 1.8 more miles — crossing Mountaineer Creek and a boulder-hop stretch near the outlet — to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.3 mi in), the last easy, reliable water before the pass. Skirt the lake's south/east shoreline on a braided, cairned climbers' path over talus and slab to the base of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep gully/headwall at the lake's south end. Aasgard Pass is the crux of the approach: it gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on a mix of dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping, cairns are frequently knocked down and the path braids into several use-trails, and well into summer it can still hold firm snow/ice that makes an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) worthwhile even though the route is otherwise a scramble. Top out at Aasgard Pass (~7,800-7,841 ft, ~5.3 mi from the trailhead). Beyond the pass, cross the grey talus/glacial-till 'moonscape' of the upper Core Zone past Tranquil Lake (Lake Freya) and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets. Near the far end of these meadows watch for an unsigned climbers' path forking right (west) toward Little Annapurna — crossing a stream and passing a toilet sign means you've overshot the junction. From there the route is more a scatter of cairned, well-worn boot paths than a trail; pick the path of least resistance up the broad north-facing slabs and talus on the peak's east/left side, switchbacking and scrambling (low 3rd class at most) to the 8,485-ft summit. Trailhead-to-summit totals run about 15-16 miles and 5,000-5,800 ft. Hazards: no water past the Colchuck Lake outlet, so fill up there; loose rock and rockfall potential on Aasgard Pass and the final slopes, especially with parties above you; full sun/thunderstorm exposure on the open talus above the pass; and early/mid-season snow on the pass creating slip-and-slide fall hazard.
descent: Reverse the North Slopes: downclimb the low-3rd-class/class-2 slabs and talus on the peak's east side back to the col/basin, pick up the braided boot paths back through the Brisingamen Lakelets meadows, and rejoin the Core Zone trail past Isolation and Tranquil Lakes to Aasgard Pass. This is a scramble walk-off in both directions — no rope, rack, or rappelling is used on the standard North Slopes line; parties simply describe reversing the ascent, and the peak is often characterized as little more than a steep class 2 hike. The one genuine descent-specific hazard is Aasgard Pass itself: down-climbing its ~2,000 ft of loose scree and talus in the afternoon (often with the sun having softened any remaining snow, and other parties ascending below) is a common cause of rockfall incidents and slips — down-climb deliberately, stay out of others' fall line, and only glissade if a real, clean snow chute with a safe runout is in (by mid-to-late summer the pass is usually bare, exposed talus rather than snow). From the base of the pass, retrace the trail around Colchuck Lake and down the Colchuck Lake/Stuart Lake Trail to the trailhead. Rappels: 0.
hazards: loose talus and slabs
the abrupt south-side drop from the summit plateau
early-season snow up high - ice axe and crampons are often needed into July
afternoon thunderstorms, most common July-August
the steep, loose Aasgard Pass headwall (about 2,000 ft of gain in ~0.5 mile) on approach and descent, with rockfall risk from parties climbing above

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, snow-free
waysIn.season: late Jul-early Oct
waysIn.notes:
Stuart Lake / Colchuck Lake Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then left/south on the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.8 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, around 4.3 miles in. That is the last easy, reliable water.

Skirt the lake's south and east shore on a braided cairned path over talus and slab to the foot of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep headwall at the lake's south end. The pass gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping. Cairns get knocked over and the path braids; there are cairns marking more than one line, so follow the most worn tread and keep climber's left of the cliff bands. Drifting climber's right toward the waterfall terrain on Colchuck Peak's flank is how people get cliffed out and killed here. Near the top the path passes a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much bigger one — missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Top out at about 7,800-7,841 ft, roughly 5.3 miles from the car. Cross the grey talus and glacial till of the upper Core past Tranquil Lake and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets.

Late September brings the larches, and with them the year's heaviest crowds and permit competition. A day scramble needs no lottery permit; camping in the Core does.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: cliffed-out terrain climber's right near the waterfalls, with fatalities on record
Misleading and duplicated cairns on the pass and on the peak itself
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above, on the pass and on the final slopes
No water past the Colchuck Lake outlet
Full sun and thunderstorm exposure on open talus above the pass — no shelter anywhere in the Core

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core with snow
waysIn.season: late Jun-mid Jul, and shoulder season either side
waysIn.notes:
The same line with snow on the pass and on the upper slopes. An ice axe is worth carrying, and sometimes crampons, even though the peak itself is a scramble — the exposure is on Aasgard, not on Little Annapurna.

Early-season snow on the pass firms overnight and turns punchy through the day, hiding ice underneath; there is also a creek running beneath the talus that snow bridges. The pass is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Descending the pass in the afternoon on softened snow, with tired legs and other parties below, is the well-documented incident scenario here. Glissade only where there is a genuine clean chute with a safe runout — by mid to late summer the pass is bare talus and there is nothing to glissade.
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges on the pass
Punchy afternoon snow over hidden ice
Patchy snow-to-slab transitions on the summit slopes
Uncontrolled glissade descending the pass — the classic afternoon incident here
waysIn.whyThisWay: Early summer and the shoulder seasons, when the pass still holds snow; same line, but bring an ice axe and crampons and take care descending the softened snow in the afternoon.

name: Northeast Face
approach: From the Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead (the Dingford Creek Trailhead, where the road is gated), follow Dutch Miller Gap Trail 1030 up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley about 14-15 miles to Dutch Miller Gap, passing Hardscrabble Horse Camp and the Williams Lake trail junction along the way. Little Big Chief sits immediately southwest of the gap, reached from the gap itself by an off-trail scramble up the peak's east slope/northeast ridge, with a short but exposed class 4 notch as the crux below the summit. An alternate, longer approach comes from the east via the Necklace Valley Trail off Foss River Road (Skykomish/US 2 side), crossing La Bohn Gap before dropping to Dutch Miller Gap. A second long approach comes from the southeast: the Waptus River Trail from Salmon La Sac to Waptus Lake (with an unbridged river ford below the lake), a ford of Chief Creek near the head of the lake, then the Dutch Miller Gap trail up past Lake Ivanhoe to the gap. For this specific route: continue the standard Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail all the way up to Dutch Miller Gap, then climb directly above the gap onto the peak's northeast ridge/face — no cross-country detour into Summit Chief Valley needed.
descent: From the summit, reverse the two short belayed pitches — using tree or sling anchors for any rappels — back into the cirque below the east face. Cross the snowfield and descend the roughly 500 feet of heather and rock steps on the northeast ridge toward Dutch Miller Gap. Parties who approached via Pete Lake/Summit Chief instead downclimb the ridge-notch crux (often roped) and drop into the northeast basin to regain camp. Do not improvise a shortcut gully: a first-hand account of this east-side face descended the East Face at class 3 but became cliffed out about 600 ft above the valley floor after straying into a northeast-trending couloir.
hazards: Lingering snow/glacier travel in the approach cirque well into summer
Loose rock on the heather/rock steps, ridge and face
Variable snowfield conditions (soft, icy, or moat-riddled) depending on season
Exposed low-5th-class crux move on the alternate northeast-basin approach
No cell coverage; a remote, rescue-difficult objective

waysIn.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap
waysIn.season: July to September; recorded ascents cluster in August and September. The upper cirque holds snow well into summer, so carry an axe.
waysIn.notes: The standard way. From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road end, follow the Dutch Miller Gap trail up the valley for a long day — roughly fourteen to fifteen miles — passing the horse camp and the Williams Lake trail junction on the way to the gap. Most parties break this over two days and camp near Williams Lake or at the gap. There is no cross-country detour for this route: stay on the trail to the top.
hazards: Snow lingering in the approach cirque well into summer, soft, icy or moat-riddled depending on the season
Loose rock on the heather and rock steps, the ridge and the face
Exposed ridge notch, class 4 and up, with a vertical-to-overhanging north side
Small, precarious summit that needs careful downclimbing
Gap is a trail high point with several ways off it; confirm the southwest side before committing
Very long trail approach (about 14-15 miles) to a remote spot with no cell coverage and difficult rescue

waysIn.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Gap from the north
waysIn.season: July to September.
waysIn.notes: A longer alternative from the other side of the divide: the Necklace Valley trail off the Foss River road, over La Bohn Gap, then down to Dutch Miller Gap. It joins the standard line at the gap, so everything above is identical. Worth knowing about mainly as a through-trip option or if the Middle Fork road end is not usable.
hazards: Long approach over a second pass, with snow on La Bohn Gap into summer
Loose rock above Dutch Miller Gap
Snow lingering in the cirque below the east face, variable conditions
Exposed ridge notch and small precarious summit as on the standard line
Remote, rescue-difficult terrain with no cell coverage
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the Middle Fork road end is unusable, or when making the climb part of a through-trip across the divide; longer, and it joins the standard line at the gap.

waysIn.name: Pete Lake and Summit Chief camp from the east
waysIn.season: July to September.
waysIn.notes: The eastern option, from a camp near Pete Lake and Summit Chief. It does not reach Dutch Miller Gap at all — it comes at the peak's northeast basin from the other side and joins the route higher up. It is the approach that puts the ridge notch in your path, which the trail-to-the-gap line avoids.
hazards: Exposed low-fifth-class crux move at the ridge notch, which most parties belay
Route-finding through the northeast basin's cliff bands
Loose rock throughout
Snowfield and cirque higher up, lingering into summer
Remote with no cell coverage
waysIn.whyThisWay: When coming from the east side or combining with Summit Chief, to reach the northeast basin without going through the gap; a different, longer way that meets the route higher up.

waysIn.name: Waptus River and Lake Ivanhoe from Salmon La Sac
waysIn.season: July to September. The river ford and the lakeshore snow are both much more serious during snowmelt.
waysIn.notes: The long southeastern way in, usually spread over two or three days. From the Salmon La Sac road end north of Cle Elum, follow the Waptus River trail up its gentle valley to Waptus Lake, roughly nine miles. The old hiker bridge over the river below the lake is gone, so this is a real ford, about knee deep at normal summer flow. Past the lake the trail follows the southeast shore, which can hold steep snow into early summer, to a ford of Chief Creek near the head of the lake, about twelve miles from the car. From Chief Creek the Dutch Miller Gap trail switchbacks up the forested slope, passes Lake Ivanhoe and reaches the gap, roughly five more miles and about 2,000 ft higher. At the gap it meets the standard approach, and the climbing above is the same.
hazards: Unbridged Waptus River ford below the lake: cold and swift, serious in snowmelt
Chief Creek ford near the head of Waptus Lake
Steep snowfields on the lake's southeast shore into early summer
Very long approach far from help, with no cell coverage
Loose rock and lingering cirque snow once at the peak, as on the standard line
waysIn.whyThisWay: When starting from the Salmon La Sac side, or on a multi-day trip through Waptus Lake; long, with a river ford that is serious at high water and steep lakeshore snow early on.

name: East Shoulder
approach: From the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead (3,800 ft) on the Sunrise/White River Road (WA-410), follow the Wonderland Trail south along Fryingpan Creek about 4.5 mi to Summerland (~5,900-5,950 ft), a subalpine meadow with a stock/hiker shelter and toilet. The Fryingpan Creek Trailhead parking area and the spur trail from it close from late September 2026 for the length of the park's Fryingpan Creek Bridge project (construction planned for 2027-2029); while they are closed, park at White River Campground and take the Wonderland Trail to Summerland. Leave the maintained trail there and climb north of Meany Crest across the Meany snowfield, making a rising traverse toward rock outcrops around 7,000-7,350 ft — the standard high camp. From camp, gain the Fryingpan Glacier, rope up, and traverse southwest to 9,100 ft Whitman Notch for the first view of the Whitman Glacier, then cross the upper Whitman Glacier to the peak's high shoulder before the final steep snow couloir and Class 3-4 summit block.
descent: Reverse the summit scramble carefully on the loose rock, then descend the glaciers along the ascent track, watching for opening crevasses later in the season.
hazards: loose volcanic rock
rockfall
crevasses
summit exposure
weakening/melted-out crevasse bridges, especially Aug-Sep
afternoon rockfall on the summit block as sun-warmed andesite loosens

waysIn.name: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun through Aug, best early July to early August — firm morning snow, drier rock, and bridges not yet melted out
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead near 3,800-3,900 ft on the Sunrise and White River Road, a few miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed trail up through old-growth beside Fryingpan Creek.

At roughly 3.2 miles and about 1,400 ft of gain there is an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek — the main water and a spot that needs care in high runoff. Continue to Summerland at about 4.5 miles and roughly 5,900 ft: patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, and the last reliable running water.

From Summerland leave maintained trail and take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll, up steep tundra and snow on the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft with flat sites and stone wind breaks. This is the standard high camp.

Above Meany Crest gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up. Climb south and southwest across the lower apron to the broad notch between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers at about 9,000-9,100 ft, then traverse and climb the upper Whitman across a bergschrund to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to rock.

The basin holds heavy snow and the approach slopes can be avalanche terrain in soft early-season conditions. Afternoon whiteout and thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.
hazards: Loose volcanic rock and rockfall on the summit gully and crest, worsening through the day
Crevasses and weakening bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, worst in August and September
Bergschrund that is a step-across early season and a problem late
Cliff-out potential between Summerland and Meany Crest if the line drifts climber's right
Avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft or early-season conditions
Major exposure on the final crest, about 2,000 ft to the Emmons on the north side
Creek crossing on a footlog that needs care in high runoff
waysIn.whyThisWay: The shorter, usual start once the Fryingpan Creek trailhead and its bridge reopen, in the early July to early August window; skips the extra walk in from White River Campground.

waysIn.name: White River Campground and the Wonderland Trail to Summerland
waysIn.notes: The Fryingpan Creek trailhead and its spur trail are closed for the bridge replacement, planned to last into 2029. Park at White River Campground, where parking is limited, and follow the Wonderland Trail to Summerland. From Summerland the climb is unchanged: the climbers' path to Meany Crest, the Fryingpan Glacier and Whitman Notch.
hazards: Trailhead and spur closed for the bridge replacement into 2029; limited parking at White River Campground
Loose volcanic rock and rockfall on the summit gully and crest, worsening through the day
Crevasses and weakening bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, worst in August and September
Cliff-out potential above Summerland if the line drifts climber's right
Avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft or early-season conditions
Major exposure on the final crest

waysIn.name: From Paradise across the Cowlitz and Ingraham glaciers
waysIn.season: Nov-May, while the White River road to Summerland is shut
waysIn.notes:
From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft. Leave it there and traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz, holding elevation to stay above the cliff and serac band below, then through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south and east face near 8,900 ft.

Camps are made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glaciers, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.

Above the ramp the route climbs the Whitman Glacier and exits its upper left-hand corner into a gully, climbs about two-thirds of it to a short step, continues up a gully-chimney to the summit notch, and finishes with a short loose scramble along the crest.

The Paradise road stays open far later into winter than the roads on the north and east sides, which is the whole reason this variant exists.
hazards: Serac fall and crevasse hazard across an extended Cowlitz and Ingraham traverse
Cliff and serac band immediately below the traverse line, so elevation must be held
Wind-slab avalanche potential on the ramp gaining the face in early season
Loose rock in the summit gully-chimney and on the final crest scramble
Long committing traverse with the same ground to reverse on the way out
Missing the 8,600 ft departure point and continuing onto the busy Camp Muir track
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late autumn through spring, while the White River road to Summerland is shut; the Paradise road stays open much later, at the cost of crossing the Cowlitz and Ingraham glaciers.

name: South Route
approach: Lizard Mountain has no trailhead of its own. It is climbed from a camp at White Rock Lakes, which parties reach from the north over the first half of the Ptarmigan Traverse and leave the same way. Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of the Cascade River Road, 23 miles from Marblemount. The maintained trail switchbacks about 3.7 miles and 1,800 ft up to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft), the last built tread of the trip. From the pass a climbers' path traverses south-southeast across the flank of Mixup Peak to the Cache Glacier; rope up for the glacier to Cache Col (~6,900 ft), then drop to Kool-Aid Lake (~6,100 ft), the usual first camp. Beyond the lake the Red Ledge crosses the cliff band, and a roped crossing of the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the gap beside Spider Mountain and down to Yang Yang Lakes (~5,800 ft). From there climb onto the Le Conte Glacier, work around Sentinel Peak, cross the broad South Cascade Glacier and top out at Lizard Col (~6,800 ft) on Lizard's south ridge, then descend to White Rock Lakes (~6,200 ft). From camp, regain the col and follow the south ridge roughly 600 vertical feet to the summit, a short but loose Class 2-3 scramble; stay near the crest to avoid the worst rubble on the flanks. Most parties take three days to reach White Rock Lakes, and the whole outing is about 35 miles round trip with some 11,000 ft of cumulative gain. The southern approach from the Downey Creek Trailhead starts with a road walk at present: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at milepost 12, about 8 miles below the trailhead; check status before planning on it.
descent: Reverse the south ridge from the summit to Lizard Col. It is loose Class 2 the whole way and needs no rappels; many parties use the west ridge as an alternative way back down to the col. From the col, drop to camp at White Rock Lakes, then retrace the approach north: across the South Cascade Glacier and around Sentinel Peak on the Le Conte Glacier to Yang Yang Lakes, over the Middle Cascade Glacier and along the Red Ledge to Kool-Aid Lake, then up to Cache Col, down the Cache Glacier and across to Cascade Pass, and down the trail to the Cascade River Road. The glaciers carry the same crevasse hazard on the way out as on the way in, and most parties take three days from White Rock Lakes back to the car.
hazards: loose blocks
lingering snow in gullies
remote self-rescue terrain (multi-day evacuation)
crevassed glacier crossings en route (Cache, Middle Cascade, and South Cascade Glaciers)
sustained off-trail bushwhacking on the Bachelor Creek exit if approaching or leaving via Downey Creek

waysIn.name: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
waysIn.season: Mid-July through September, once the Cache Col snow has consolidated and the Red Ledge is clear of verglas; the whole corridor has to be in condition, not just the peak.
waysIn.notes: Lizard has no trailhead of its own and is normally met partway through the high traverse rather than approached. From the Cascade River Road end, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and then traverses meadow and talus to Cascade Pass, which is the last built tread of the trip. Leave it there and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow to the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, then drop the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. Beyond, the Red Ledge cuts the cliff band west of Art's Knoll, then the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the Spider-Formidable col and down to Yang Yang Lakes. From there the line climbs past Le Conte Mountain, crosses the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, and crosses the South Cascade Glacier to the col at its head before dropping into the White Rock Lakes basin. Lizard is the side trip from that camp: climb back out of the basin northeast to the broad notch on the peak's south ridge.
hazards: Roped glacier travel on the Cache, Middle Cascade, Le Conte and South Cascade Glaciers, with crevasses opening through late season
Steep heather above the Cache Col descent, where a slip runs out onto rock
Red Ledge can hold an open moat, verglas or fresh snow well into summer
Whiteout navigation at the Spider-Formidable col, with no bail once past Cache Col
Loose blocks on the summit ridge
Lingering snow in gullies; remote, multi-day evacuation with no cell coverage

waysIn.name: From the south — Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek (road closed at milepost 12)
waysIn.season: Late July through September. The Bachelor Creek brush is worst before the snow has settled it and the Bachelor Creek ford is worst during peak melt.
waysIn.notes: The Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at milepost 12 under a Forest Service order in effect since November 5, 2026, about 8 miles below the Downey Creek Trailhead, so this way starts with a road walk or ride; fire closures have also affected the trailhead and the Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek trails in recent seasons, so check current alerts. This is the other end of the same corridor. From the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, Downey Creek Trail #768 enters wilderness within the first half mile and climbs gently through old growth, crossing tributary creeks that run high in early season, to the Bachelor Creek junction. The Bachelor Creek path is unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown, with an alder and slide-alder band around 3,800 to 4,400 ft that becomes a genuine bushwhack when snow has not flattened it. It fords Bachelor Creek itself, which runs fast and cold with snowmelt. Above treeline the tread breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake, reliable water and a common first camp. A steep, often snow-covered pitch gains Itswoot Ridge; from there the route climbs to Spire Col, descends the Dana Glacier to White Rock Lakes, and regains the col on Lizard's south ridge from the lakes.
hazards: Road closed to vehicles 8 miles below the trailhead; check status before planning
Sustained blowdown and slide-alder bushwhacking on the Bachelor Creek path
Bachelor Creek ford during snowmelt
Crevasse hazard on the Dana Glacier below Spire Col
Multi-day evacuation distance with no cell coverage
Loose blocks near the summit crest, lingering snow in gullies
waysIn.whyThisWay: When starting from the south end of the corridor or finishing a through-trip, with 8 miles of closed road to walk or bike; brushy Bachelor Creek and a cold fast ford make it harder at peak melt.

name: East Slopes
approach: From the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft, at the end of White River Road/FR 6400, reached via WA-207 and White River Road from Coles Corner off US-2), follow the White River Trail (#1507) upstream along a mostly level grade through old-growth forest for about 4 miles to its junction with the Boulder Pass Trail (#1562, also called the Boulder Creek Trail). Water is abundant the whole way — the White River parallels the trail, and Boulder Creek is a dependable source at the junction (the crossing here can be a ford depending on the year/season, so check recent trip reports before committing). Turn onto the Boulder Pass Trail and climb switchbacks through forest, gaining roughly 2,500-2,700 ft over about 3 miles to break out into the open basin below Boulder Pass (~5,000 ft). Because the round trip from the trailhead runs in the 20+ mile range with well over 6,000 ft of gain, most parties do this as an overnight, camping in the Boulder Pass basin or pushing on to a high camp in Upper Boulder Basin (~5,800 ft). From the basin, leave the maintained trail for the unmaintained 'sheepherder's path,' a boot track that sidehills west across a series of cirques (Clark Basin, then Luahna Basin), losing roughly 1,000 ft as it traverses below Clark Mountain's south spur before regaining elevation near a 7,200 ft spur. This traverse is the route-finding crux of the approach — brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in poor visibility or snow cover. From the spur, a rising traverse across broad benches (often snow-covered well into summer) and easy Class 2 ledges leads to the ~7,600 ft col west of Clark Mountain; from there a rising traverse across the upper Richardson Glacier (real crevasse hazard — carry glacier travel gear, and note the glacier has been reported thinning/broken-up and less straightforward in recent years) reaches Luahna's East Ridge, which is scrambled west to the summit.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the East Ridge scrambling back to the top of the short, steep rock step below it — parties describe this step as low Class 4 and sometimes icy/verglassed in an adjacent gully. Strong parties down-climb it, but a short single-rope rappel (one rappel, roughly 20-30m/60-90ft, off a natural anchor — webbing/tat around a horn or block; no bolted or fixed-chain anchor has been reported) is common practice here, especially for less-experienced members or when the step is wet or icy. Below the step, re-cross the upper Richardson Glacier traverse to the 7,600 ft col, then reverse the Clark/Luahna cirque sheepherder's-path traverse back to the Boulder Pass basin, picking up the maintained Boulder Pass Trail (#1562) down to the White River Trail (#1507) and out to the trailhead. Some parties instead exit via Thunder Creek — dropping south from the summit/basin directly into the Thunder Creek drainage — but parties describe that alternative as slower and rougher, with heavy blowdown and avalanche debris in the basin and an overgrown, disappearing boot path near the creek crossing and the White River Trail junction; reversing the ascent line via Boulder Pass is the more reliable descent for most parties. This is fundamentally a walk-off/downclimb approach with at most one short technical rappel at the rock step — not a multi-rappel technical descent.
hazards: loose scree and rotten rock, especially just below the summit block
unmaintained route above roughly 5,700 ft — a faint sheepherder's path and cross-country travel with genuine route-finding difficulty
a brief class 3-4 step on the ridge, sometimes bypassed on exposed ledges
moat hazards where the route crosses the upper Richardson Glacier margin
dense bushwhacking and avalanche/blowdown debris in the Boulder Creek and Thunder Creek drainages
early-season steep snow and avalanche terrain on approach slopes
very remote, multi-hour approach with serious self-rescue and evacuation implications; no cell coverage

waysIn.name: Boulder Pass and the sheepherder's traverse to the col west of Clark Mountain, then the upper Richardson Glacier
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, with August the most reliable. The Richardson has been reported thinning and breaking up in recent years, so a late-season party should expect it to be less straightforward than it used to be
waysIn.notes: From the White River Trailhead near 2,300 ft at the end of FR-6400, White River Trail #1507 runs almost level upstream through old growth for about four miles. The junction with Boulder Creek Trail #1562 sits roughly a quarter mile past the bridge over Boulder Creek — if you have crossed the creek and seen no sign, keep walking. Turn onto #1562 and climb gently through forest to the established camp at the creek crossing near 3,700 ft; whether that is a step-across or a genuine ford depends on the year. Above camp the trail switchbacks and climbs roughly 2,500-2,700 ft over about three miles into the open basin below Boulder Pass. Snow lingers in that basin well into summer, and the basin is where the route leaves the maintained trail for an unmaintained sheepherder's path that sidehills west across a series of cirques, losing roughly 1,000 ft as it traverses below Clark Mountain's south spur before regaining height near a 7,200 ft spur. That traverse is the route-finding crux of the approach: brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in poor visibility or under snow.
hazards: Crevasses and moats on an upper Richardson Glacier that recent parties report thinning and breaking up
The sheepherder's traverse across the cirques — brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in cloud or snow
A short low Class 4 step below the east ridge that can carry verglas and has no fixed anchor
Loose scree and rotten rock just below the summit block
A Thunder Creek exit that reads shorter on the map and is documented as slower, brushier and harder to follow

name: Luna Glacier
approach: Reaching Luna Cirque is the crux of the trip. The historical approach follows the Big Beaver Trail from Ross Lake (the Ross Lake Resort water taxi, charged per boat, cuts about 6 miles off the hike) up to Luna Camp, then climbs steeply beside Luna Creek into the cirque — the bushwhack is a notoriously miserable fight through flies, devil's club, willows, and alder. Most contemporary parties instead approach via Access Creek, which branches off that same Big Beaver Trail rather than a separate trailhead — parties continue on the maintained trail a mile to a mile and a half past Luna Camp to the unmarked Access Creek/Big Beaver Creek confluence, then leave the trail there to follow the Access Creek drainage (with an occasional bootpath) up into the cirque — a longer but far less brutal line than Luna Creek.
descent: Reverse the route: downclimb or rappel off the summit block, reverse the slab pitches to the top of the highest snowfield, downclimb the rock step, and descend the hanging glacier roped and protected with pickets/flukes back into Luna Cirque and high camp.
hazards: Hanging glacier crux can be broken, thin, or impassable in late season
Loose rock on the step above the glacier
Exposed, unprotected traverse across the summit block
Fast-moving fog/whiteout common on the ridge, complicating route-finding
Brutal, insect-plagued bushwhack if the Luna Creek approach is used

waysIn.name: Big Beaver Trail and Access Creek into Luna Cirque, rather than the Luna Creek bushwhack
waysIn.season: Jun to early Aug. The hanging glacier is the crux of the route and can be impassable in late season, which is why the window is early
waysIn.notes:
Reaching Luna Cirque is the crux of the trip. The historical line follows the Big Beaver Trail from Ross Lake, with a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort cutting about 6 miles off the hike, up to Luna Camp, then climbs steeply beside Luna Creek into the cirque. That bushwhack is a notoriously miserable struggle with flies, devil's club, willows and alder.

Most contemporary parties instead approach via Access Creek, which branches off the same Big Beaver Trail rather than a separate trailhead. Continue on maintained trail past Luna Camp to the unmarked Access Creek and Big Beaver Creek confluence, then leave the trail and follow the Access Creek drainage, with an occasional bootpath, up into the cirque. Longer, and far less brutal.
hazards: A hanging glacier that is the route's crux and can be impassable in late season
The Luna Creek approach, if chosen, is among the worst brush in the Cascades
Sparse protection on the slab pitches
Recrossing the glacier on the descent, on the same conditions that decided the ascent

name: Southwest Ridge
approach: From the Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20 milepost 134), cross Ross Dam and work around the lake to the Big Beaver Trail, or save about 7 miles by taking the lake boat shuttle to Big Beaver landing. Follow Big Beaver Trail past Luna Camp, roughly 10 miles up from the landing, and leave it about 1.5 miles beyond the camp at a big cairn on the left. Drop through forest to Big Beaver Creek, ford it since logs are not dependable, then traverse southwest through alder thickets to the head of Access Creek, crossing it near 3900 ft and camping in the meadow near 4200 ft. From there climb about 2000 ft of loose gully to the col that opens onto the southwest ridge, and make an ascending traverse to the next col at the edge of the ridge, where the climbing starts.
descent: Descend the way you came. From the summit, work back along the ramps and ledges on the southeast side to the false summit, then downclimb the class 3 rock of the southwest ridge to the col. The step between the two summits is very exposed and a fall there would be fatal, so move carefully and avoid wet rock. From the col, retrace the traverse to the upper col and descend the gully to the Access Creek meadows, which becomes a loose rock pile late in the season, so stay close together or out of each other's fall line and wear helmets. Then bushwhack back to Big Beaver Creek, ford it, and walk the Big Beaver trail out to the Ross Lake landing.
hazards: extreme remoteness — a multi-day, largely off-trail approach with no cell coverage; a serious injury near the summit realistically requires helicopter evacuation, not a ground carry-out
brushy, steep approach through the Access Creek basin choked with devil's club and slide alder; the first off-trail quarter-mile alone can take over an hour
cold, thigh-to-waist-deep fords of Big Beaver Creek and Access Creek
lingering snow/ice in the gullies to Access Col and on Luna Pass well into July
~4,000 ft of sustained, continuous exposure on the Class 3–4 traverse between the false and true summits
sparse cairns and genuine route-finding difficulty across the cross-country basins in poor visibility
ground-nesting bees/wasps encountered by multiple parties in the forested sections

waysIn.name: Access Creek basin, then the gap south of Point 6,730 and the 6,600 ft basin traverse to Luna Col
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The trip starts at the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 at about 2,050 ft, with parking right off the highway. About 0.8 mile of trail leads down to Ross Lake, then a boat shuttle roughly 9 miles up-lake to the Big Beaver Trailhead at about 1,600 ft. The lake crossing is a logistical step rather than an afterthought, since the resort's shuttle season and hours govern when you can reach the trailhead at all.

From the Big Beaver Trailhead, about 8 miles of well-graded trail through old-growth cedar along the north bank of Big Beaver Creek reach Luna Camp. Continue roughly 1.5 miles past it and watch on the left for a small, easy-to-miss boot path leaving the maintained trail just north of where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek at about 2,460 ft. Ford Big Beaver Creek there.

Around 3,700 ft the brush thickens; cross to the south bank of Access Creek, where intermittent cairns and a faint path use talus benches to dodge the worst of the slide alder and devil's club. This stretch is the approach crux. The path deposits you in the open basin at the Access Creek headwaters at about 4,400 ft, the common base camp.
hazards: Sustained bushwhacking, blowdown and route-finding in the Access Creek drainage, the approach crux
A ford of Big Beaver Creek that can run high with snowmelt
A narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest between the false and true summits, with cliffs on both sides
Loose talus and scree on the upper ridge with rockfall risk onto parties below
No reliable water above the Access Creek camp except lingering snowmelt
Losing the boot path in poor light on the way down, which several trip reports record

name: South Face Left
approach: Follow the Commonwealth Creek trail (PCT to Commonwealth Creek trail) until soon after crossing a stream and moving onto the flank of Red Mountain; leave the trail and follow the side valley below Lundin up to the base of its south face.
descent: The route tops out on the West Ridge a short way below the summit. Either reverse the West Ridge, Class 3-4 with a few low fifth-class moves, rappelling or downclimbing most of it to the notch near 5,800 ft at its foot and dropping back into Commonwealth Basin; or descend the Southeast Ridge to Red Pass (about 5,400 ft), Class 3-4 with one rappel of about 80 ft, then follow the Commonwealth Basin trail about 4.5 miles back to the trailhead.
hazards: The opening layback hand crack has been reported wet even when the rest of the face is dry — allow drying time after storms.
Lundin's rock becomes unsafe when wet; the South Face routes should not be attempted damp.
Loose rock and talus on the peak generally, especially hazardous while descending scree — a fatal fall on descent is documented (1980).
Lingering snow in the south couloir into July can require self-arrest skills on the approach or descent.

name: West Ridge
approach: Two standard ways to reach the base of the West Ridge, both converging on the ridge's low-point notch around 5,800 ft where the technical climbing starts. (1) Commonwealth/Lundin Basin approach: from the PCT-North/Commonwealth Basin trailhead off Alpental Rd (elev. ~3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; within about half a mile bear left onto the Commonwealth Basin use-trail, which climbs gently along Commonwealth Creek through old-growth forest for roughly 1.7 mi as the valley opens into the basin. Near 4,200 ft, leave the main Red Pass/Commonwealth Basin tread and cut left (west), contouring into Lundin Basin below Red Mountain's south face. From there climb a broad couloir (snow early season, scree/talus by late summer) up Lundin's steep south face to gain the West Ridge at the obvious saddle/notch. This leg runs roughly 3.5-4 miles one-way with about 2,800 ft of gain, 2.5-3 hours. Commonwealth Creek is a reliable water source in the lower basin but nothing is dependable once you're up in Lundin Basin, so top off early. Hazards: the south-face couloir is prone to wet-slide/sluffing in afternoon sun and wants an axe (crampons if firm) in early season; the basin traverse can be brushy, boulder-hop route-finding once snow melts out late in the season. (2) Cave Ridge/Alpental approach (faster, and the better late-season option since it skirts the brushy lower basin): park at the Alpental day-use lot and find the unmarked, unmaintained 'Snoqualmie Mountain' climbers' trail beginning about 50 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead. It crosses below a small waterfall and climbs steeply through forest and slide alder to an unsigned split around 4,600 ft where paths fork toward Snoqualmie Mountain, Cave Ridge, and Lundin. Take the Cave Ridge/Lundin fork, cross over Cave Ridge near its low notch, then follow an ascending climbers'-trail traverse below the ridge crest (staying on the Commonwealth Basin/north side) to the West Ridge notch. About 2.5-3 miles one-way, ~2,800-3,000 ft gain; trip reports clock roughly 2.5-4 hours trailhead-to-ridge-base. No reliable water past the trailhead. Hazards: exposed, sometimes loose climbers'-trail traverse under Cave Ridge, and an early-season snow traverse that can warrant an axe.
descent: Most parties reverse the West Ridge: from the true (west) summit, downclimb the class 3-4 ridge crest back toward the notch/saddle used on the way up, staying on the north side of the crest per the standard line and reversing the short crux step (a ~6 ft downclimb at a minor notch). Many parties downclimb this cleanly, but a single short rappel (roughly 15 m/50 ft, well within a 30 m single-rope length) is commonly used here instead, especially in wet conditions or with less experienced climbers — anchors are natural (slung horns/blocks or a small nut/cam placement backed by a cordelette), not bolted; there's no fixed hardware on this route. From the saddle, either reverse the ascent couloir into Lundin Basin (a fast glissade of up to 1,200-1,500 ft when it's still snow-filled, typically only reliable early season) or walk scree/talus down toward the Red-Lundin col to pick up the use trail back into Commonwealth Basin and the PCT. An alternative some parties use is descending the East Ridge instead: scramble down the crest about 100 ft to the top of a small cliff band, then make one single-rope rappel (30 m is sufficient; natural tree/horn anchors — the ridge has plenty of trees to sling) down to easy ledges, continuing to a notch in the ridge crest from which an early-season glissade or scramble rejoins the standard route in Lundin/Commonwealth Basin. This option requires either looping back on foot into Commonwealth Basin or a car shuttle/hitch between the Alpental and PCT-North trailheads, since the two approaches start at different lots. Bottom line for planning: expect zero to one short rappel (under 15 m, single rope, natural gear anchors — no bolts) — conditions and party comfort level determine whether it's downclimbed or rapped. Total descent to the trailhead runs roughly 2-2.5 hours. To make a loop, descend the east ridge from July to September: a short class 2-3 walk leads to the rappel anchors (about 35 to 40 m to easy ground), then a boot path drops to the saddle with East Lundin and over to Red Pass.
hazards: loose rock/talus, especially hazardous while descending scree (documented fatal fall, 1980)
exposed, unprotected summit step with low-5th moves
rock becomes unsafe when wet — do not attempt the South Face routes damp
lingering snow in the south couloir into July can require self-arrest skill
a roughly 30-ft downclimb around a gendarme on the West Ridge turns many parties back short of the true summit

waysIn.name: Commonwealth Basin and Lundin Basin
waysIn.season: Jun-Jul on snow is the good window; brushy and slow once melted out
waysIn.notes:
From the PCT-North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead off the Alpental road (about 3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; within roughly half a mile bear left onto the Commonwealth Basin use trail, which climbs gently along Commonwealth Creek through old-growth for about 1.7 miles as the valley opens out.
