Near 4,200 ft leave the main Red Pass tread and cut west, contouring into Lundin Basin below Red Mountain's south face. From there climb a broad couloir — snow in early season, scree and talus by late summer — up the steep south side of Lundin to gain the West Ridge at its notch.

This is much the better line while snow still covers the basin: it buries the brush and the boulders, and parties report a long glissade on the way out. Once melted out the lower basin is brushy with steep scree and talus, and that is the reason many parties switch to the Cave Ridge approach late in the season.

Commonwealth Creek is reliable water low down; nothing above is dependable, so fill up in the basin.
hazards: Wet-slide and sluffing in the south-face couloir under afternoon sun; early-season snow needs an axe, crampons if firm
Heavy brush and steep loose scree in the basin once the snow is gone
No reliable water above Commonwealth Creek
Ridge unsafe when wet and unsafe without rock gear
Exposed, unprotected summit step with low-5th moves
Loose rock and scree, especially dangerous on the descent

waysIn.name: Cave Ridge traverse from Alpental
waysIn.season: Jul-Oct; the better late-season option
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Alpental day-use lot and find the unmarked, unmaintained Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail that starts about 50 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead. It crosses below a small waterfall and climbs steeply through forest and slide alder.

At an unsigned split around 4,600 ft, paths fork toward Snoqualmie Mountain, Cave Ridge and Lundin. Take the Cave Ridge / Lundin fork, cross over Cave Ridge near its low notch, then follow an ascending climbers'-trail traverse below the ridge crest — staying on the Commonwealth Basin, north, side — to the West Ridge notch.

This skirts the brushy lower basin entirely, which is why parties prefer it once the snow has gone. There is no reliable water past the trailhead.
hazards: Exposed and sometimes loose climbers'-trail traverse beneath Cave Ridge
Early-season snow traverse on the crossing that can warrant an axe
Unsigned trail split around 4,600 ft with three destinations
Slide alder low down
Exposed, unprotected summit step with low-5th moves; ridge unsafe when wet
Loose rock and scree, especially dangerous on the descent
waysIn.whyThisWay: Late season, once the snow has melted out and the Commonwealth Basin turns to brush and loose scree and talus; it skirts that lower basin entirely.

name: South Ridge / Southeast Slopes
approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,660 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), follow the Cascade Pass Trail — a well-graded, heavily switchbacked National Park trail — 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft of gain to Cascade Pass (5,360-5,400 ft), the low notch between Mixup Peak and Cascade Peak. This section is on-trail, well-marked, and passable by early-to-mid summer once the switchbacks melt out; it's also the most crowded stretch since it's a popular day hike in its own right. At the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up a climber's path bearing south-southeast, making a rising traverse across open heather and snow benches on the east flank of Mixup Peak. This climber's trail is intermittent and route-finding becomes more important in early season when it's snow-covered. Continue the traverse to the base of the Cache Glacier (~6,000 ft), then ascend moderate snow slopes (up to about 35 degrees) to Cache Col (6,900-6,960 ft); the glacier here is small and generally reported free of significant crevasse hazard, but an ice axe and sometimes crampons are worth carrying for the snow slope depending on season and firmness. From Cache Col, descend roughly 600 ft on a climber's path with a descending traverse to the southeast, dropping to Kool-Aid Lake (about 6,120 ft), the standard camp/bivy area for Magic Mountain and the broader Ptarmigan Traverse. From Kool-Aid Lake, the final approach climbs about 1,000 ft directly up heather and scree slopes to the col (~7,100 ft) separating Magic Mountain from neighboring Hurry Up Peak, which is where the South Ridge proper begins. There is reliable water at Kool-Aid Lake and seasonal snowmelt along the traverse, but none on the upper ridge itself. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at the trailhead and a backcountry camping permit is required from North Cascades National Park for overnight stays at Kool-Aid Lake; most parties treat this as a 2-day trip with a camp at the lake rather than a car-to-car push given the off-trail navigation. Water at Kool-Aid Lake is plentiful in early August but tastes stale, so treat it.
descent: Descent reverses the ascent line down the South Ridge. From the true summit (7,610 ft), climb back down the Class 3-4 broken ledges that corkscrew the east side of the summit tower, then climb back up the roughly 80 ft dirty gully to the false summit (about 300 ft southeast of the true summit) before continuing down the easy heather/scree of the South Ridge to the Magic Mountain-Hurry Up col. This corkscrew section is the technical crux of the whole outing — loose, broken rock with real exposure — and is where the route's single rappel comes in: many parties downclimb it as Class 3-4 with a spotting belay, but a short single-rope rappel (roughly 50-80 ft, well within a 30m or 60m single strand, or a doubled 30m rope) off a natural anchor — a sling around a horn or chockstone, since there are no bolts or fixed hardware reported on this remote, lightly-traveled summit — is commonly used by parties wanting to avoid down-climbing the loose ledges, especially in wet or snowy conditions. From the col, retrace the approach: down to Kool-Aid Lake, back up and over Cache Col, down the Cache Glacier snow slopes and the Mixup Peak traverse to Cascade Pass, then out the maintained Cascade Pass Trail to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock on the corkscrew ledges and the upper gully, and for soft/rotten snow on the Cache Glacier descent later in the day — this is a route best started early to avoid downclimbing softened snow on the return.
hazards: loose, blocky rock on the Class 3-4 summit tower ledges
crevasse hazard crossing the (small) Cache Glacier en route to Cache Col
steep, sometimes icy snow on the Cache Col traverse in early/late season
route-finding difficulty on the unmaintained climber's path from Cascade Pass to Kool-Aid Lake, especially in poor visibility
fast-changing marine-climate weather in the Cache Col/Kool-Aid Lake basin

waysIn.name: Cascade Pass, Cache Col and Kool-Aid Lake
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road, follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and roughly 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft. This stretch is well graded, well marked and by far the busiest — it is a popular day hike in its own right.

At the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up the climbers' path to climber's right, bearing south-southeast. It makes a rising traverse over snow or heather across the east flanks of Mixup Peak, crossing a spur ridge, to the base of the Cache Glacier at about 6,000 ft. The path is intermittent and in early season it is under snow, when route-finding matters more and the traverse has a bad runout.

Ascend moderate snow — up to about 35 degrees — to Cache Col at roughly 6,900-6,960 ft. The glacier here is small and generally reported free of significant crevasse hazard, but carry an axe and often crampons depending on firmness. Late season Cache Col itself can moat out and become awkward to cross.

From Cache Col make a descending traverse south-southeast, losing about 600 ft, to Kool-Aid Lake at about 6,120 ft — the standard camp for Magic Mountain and for the Ptarmigan Traverse, with reliable water. Most parties treat this as a two-day trip rather than a car-to-car push.

A Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking; overnight camping at Kool-Aid Lake needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, picked up in person at Marblemount for the Cascade River Road areas.
hazards: Snow-covered traverse below Mixup with a poor runout in early season
Cache Col moats out and becomes awkward late season
Loose rock on the summit tower ledges
The false summit — parties stop there or commit to the wrong side of it
No water on the upper ridge; last reliable source is Kool-Aid Lake

name: West Ridge
approach: Approach via the general Cascade Pass/Ptarmigan Traverse access to reach the pocket glacier below Magic Mountain's west face.
descent: From the summit, walk off down the South Ridge: downclimb the Class 3-4 ledges around the east side of the summit tower, regain the false summit, and follow the ridge to the Magic-Hurry-up col above Kool-Aid Lake. Reversing the route is the alternative: reverse the chimney and slab, downclimb the open book, and re-cross the schrund back to the pocket glacier.
hazards: Bergschrund crossing hazard below the west face, difficulty varies by year

waysIn.name: The pocket glacier under the west face, and the schrund that guards it
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, with the bergschrund crossing and the pocket-glacier conditions varying by snow year
waysIn.notes:
Approach by the general Cascade Pass and Ptarmigan Traverse access: Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, the trail to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then the climbers' path across Mixup Peak's flanks, over the Cache Glacier and Cache Col near 6,900 ft, and down toward the Kool-Aid Lake basin.

From the basin, easy slopes on the west-southwest side lead to the small pocket glacier under Magic Mountain's west face. That pocket glacier is the base area, and the bergschrund at its head is where the route begins.

About four pitches: shelves to a blocky open book, the 5.6 open book, the slab taken on its easier left side, and an easy chimney on the left to gain the crest between the false and main summits.
hazards: A bergschrund below the west face whose difficulty varies by year and which can be the crux of the route by late summer
A crevassed Cache Glacier on the approach, about 35 degrees and bare ice late season
Broken gneiss with slung blocks for belays and no fixed gear
A thin slab pitch where protection is limited

name: West Route
approach: From the Trinity Trailhead (~2,820 ft, at the end of Chiwawa River/Chiwawa Valley Road, Forest Road 6200, reached via Coles Corner and Hwy 207), pick up the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 and follow it upstream through forest for roughly 4 miles. Watch the left (west) side of the trail for an 'M' blazed/carved into a tree — this marks the unsigned, unmaintained sheepherder's path up to Massie Lake, and it's easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. Ford the Chiwawa River at this point (can run cold and pushy with snowmelt into early summer; trekking poles help, expect wet feet) and pick up the old sheep-drive trail, which climbs steeply via a mix of tree blazes and intermittent boot-track for about 2 miles to Massie Lake (about 5,900 ft), a clear trout-holding tarn with a couple of established campsites. There is essentially no reliable water between the river ford and the lake, so fill up at the Chiwawa. From Massie Lake, continue on the faint sheep/game-trail tread of the Massie Lake High Route, contouring northwest roughly 1.5 miles toward Pass No Pass, then leave that trail and turn uphill (climber's right) onto Massie Peak's broad west ridge. Follow the ridge crest east for a bit over a mile — talus and heather with a few short rock steps, generally Class 2 with brief Class 3 moves near the summit block — to the 7,533 ft summit. The main hazard throughout is route-finding: the sheepherder path disappears in places, blazes thin out above treeline, and the entire line beyond the Chiwawa River Trail is off-trail, unsigned, and easy to lose in flat light — bring a map/GPS track. Snow and ice can linger on shaded sections of the high route and ridge well into summer; many parties carry microspikes and a light ice axe for trips before mid-July.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the west ridge (Class 2-3, some loose rock underfoot) back to the point where you gained it from the Massie Lake High Route, rejoin that faint tread and follow it back southeast to Massie Lake, then descend the steep sheepherder path back down to the Chiwawa River ford and out the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 to Trinity Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route — there are no fixed anchors reported on Massie Peak's west ridge or the approach gully, consistent with its Class 2-3 scrambling character. The trickiest part of the descent is simply staying on the correct (badly faded) line: the sheep trail is easy to lose both up in the high-route traverse and on the steep drop back to the river, and a mistaken line can dead-end in cliff bands or brush. Some parties instead continue past Massie Lake and pick a 'route of least resistance' down open slopes directly to Buck Creek Trail when linking Massie Peak with neighboring summits (Mount Cleator, Helmet Butte, Liberty Cap) on a multi-day loop, but for a straightforward out-and-back on the West Route, reversing the ascent line described above is the standard descent.
hazards: loose scree
remote terrain
unsigned, unmaintained climber's trail — easy to lose, especially on the descent
biting insects (mosquitoes/flies) at Massie Lake in mid-summer
fast-changing mountain weather with common summer afternoon thunderstorms
short exposed class 3 (locally near class 4) moves on the direct ridge crest

waysIn.name: Chiwawa River Trail to the sheepherder's path and Massie Lake
waysIn.season: The high country here is typically not fully snow-free until mid to late July; shaded sections of the high route and ridge hold snow and ice well into summer.
waysIn.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the Chiwawa valley, fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit and follow the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 upstream through forest, watching the west side of the tread for the marker described below. Ford the river at that point — it can run thigh-deep and swift with early-season snowmelt, so cross in the morning when flows are lowest — and pick up the old sheep-drive path, which climbs steeply on a mix of axe and burn blazes and intermittent boot track to Massie Lake. There is essentially no reliable water between the ford and the lake. From the lake the faint sheep and game tread of the high route contours northwest toward the pass ahead; leave it and turn uphill onto the peak's broad west ridge.
hazards: A false set of markers has existed roughly a mile short of the real junction and cost a party hours of bushwhacking
Unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River, thigh-deep and swift during snowmelt, with driftwood piles the only aid
Route-finding is the main hazard: the sheepherder path disappears in places and the whole line beyond the river trail is unsigned
Snow and ice on shaded sections of the high route and ridge into midsummer
No reliable water between the river and the lake

name: Southwest Scramble
approach: From Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road (Forest Road 7600) about 4.2–4.3 miles west to the Snow Lakes Trailhead and parking area on the south side of the road (~1,350 ft). Start on the Snow Lakes Trail No. 1553, which climbs steadily through forest along Icicle Creek/Snow Creek drainage. About 5.3 miles in you pass Nada Lake, with a loud waterfall/creek blast just above it that's a reliable water source; continue to Lower and Upper Snow Lakes, where a logjam between the two lakes is a known crossing hazard (especially at high water or in the dark on an alpine start). Beyond the Snow Lakes the trail (now a rougher climbers' path) switchbacks steeply up into the core Enchantments basin, passing Lake Viviane, then Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes — by this point you've covered roughly 9–10 miles and gained most of the route's elevation. At the flat, open area at ~7,000 ft between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes, leave the maintained trail and head south-southeast, aiming for McClellan Ridge and staying west of a distinctive rock tower known as "the Prong." Ascend steep talus, scree, or snow (depending on season — often firm/icy in late summer and fall, so an axe/microspikes are worth carrying) to gain the ridge crest. This upper section has no reliable water and involves real route-finding; a permit is required to camp overnight in the core Enchantments zone (May 15-Oct 31).
descent: This route's crux move is on the ridge itself, not a technical descent: from the ridge crest (reached via the ascent line west of the Prong), drop roughly 70 vertical feet off the crest and wrap around to the south side of McClellan Peak, then scramble up class 3 rock to the true summit. Descend by reversing this exact sequence: downclimb the class 3 south-side rock back to the ~70-ft notch below the ridge crest, regain the crest, and drop back down the steep talus/scree/snow slope west of the Prong to the flat area between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes at ~7,000 ft. From there, rejoin the Snow Lakes Trail (No. 1553) and retrace it past Lake Viviane, the Snow Lakes, and Nada Lake back to the trailhead — summit-to-trailhead typically takes roughly 5–5.5 hours. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required. Watch for loose rock and exposure on the class 3 downclimb (parties have noted going down 20 ft and wrapping to an easier gully when the direct line felt too exposed), ice on the ridge slope in late season, and the same logjam crossing between the Snow Lakes on the way out. Carry an axe/microspikes if snow lingers on the upper slope, since a slip there has real runout consequences.
hazards: loose talus and granite blocks
route-finding across the broad massif and its subsidiary towers (the Prong, the Pawn)
cliffing out on the steeper southwest slabs/chimney if the easier south/southeast line is missed
afternoon thunderstorms over exposed ridge and summit block
steep, sometimes icy snow finger below the Prong notch in early or late season
footbridge/creek crossing near Nada Lake can be swift and exposed at high spring flow
long single-day car-to-car pushes (~24 mi) are common due to competitive overnight permits, raising fatigue and turnaround-time risk

waysIn.name: Snow Lakes to the core basin, then McClellan Ridge past the Prong
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; late-season the slope below the ridge often goes icy
waysIn.notes:
Snow Lakes Trailhead on Icicle Road about 4.2 miles from Leavenworth. Snow Lakes Trail #1553 climbs steadily through forest, passing Nada Lake at roughly 5.3 miles, then Lower and Upper Snow Lakes — the logjam between the two lakes is the known crossing hazard, especially at high water or on a pre-dawn start.

Above the Snow Lakes the tread coarsens into a climbers' path and switchbacks steeply into the core basin past Lake Viviane, then Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes. By this point most of the day's elevation is behind you.

Leave the trail at the flat, open ground around 7,000 ft between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes and head south-southeast for McClellan Ridge.
hazards: The logjam crossing between Lower and Upper Snow Lakes, worst at high water or in the dark
Steep snow below the ridge that turns firm and icy in late season — an axe or microspikes are worth carrying
Loose talus and scree gaining the ridge
No water above the basin lakes
Real route-finding with no trail on the upper half

name: Summit Block Scramble (from Stehekin)
approach: McGregor Mountain is only reachable via Stehekin, at the head of Lake Chelan, which has no outside road access — get there by the Lady of the Lake ferry, floatplane, or the long trail from Cascade Pass/Bridge Creek. From Stehekin Landing, take the NPS shuttle bus (or walk/bike) 11 miles up the Stehekin Valley Road to its end at High Bridge (a hiking permit is required for the overnight version of this trip). From High Bridge, follow the Old Wagon Road/PCT north to Howard Lake at about 1.3 miles; the signed junction where the McGregor Mountain Trail forks right is just beyond the lake — Howard Lake is a reliable water source and a good gut-check that you're on route. Beyond the lake the trail switchbacks relentlessly (climbers report close to 100 switchbacks) up through forest and rocky slopes that get hot and dry with little shade or water, gaining well over 5,000 ft over the next 5.5-6 miles to Heaton Camp at about 6,700 ft, a small single-party designated site where a seasonal-snowmelt stream just below camp is the last dependable water before the summit push. From Heaton Camp the maintained trail continues another quarter- to half-mile to where it ends at the base of a talus field; total stats to the true summit are about 7.75 miles and 6,600 ft one-way. The final roughly 1,000-1,100 vertical feet is an exposed Class 2-3 scramble, not a trail: intermittent (and often faded) red arrows painted on the rock mark the line, which loops right then left behind a lower sub-summit, crosses a snowfield/talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier, then follows a fairly level shoulder past an old radio installation to the true summit and former fire-lookout site. Carry an ice axe if snow still covers the talus or the shelf above the glacier (common into midsummer), and expect loose rock ('kitty litter' on slabs) and real exposure on the ledges near the top — staying precisely on the arrow-marked line matters, as it gets noticeably dicier off-route.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route. Reverse the scramble exactly: downclimb the ledgy, loose upper 1,000-1,100 ft back along the red-arrow line past the Sandalee Glacier snowfield/talus shelf and around the lower sub-summit to the top of the main talus field below Heaton Camp. Multiple trip reports specifically flag the descent as the more dangerous half of the trip — loose, gravelly ('kitty litter') slab sections sit right above significant exposure, so downclimb deliberately, stay right on the marked route, and consider a helmet for the scramble portion. Once back on maintained trail at Heaton Camp, it's a long reversal of the approach: roughly 6-7 miles and nearly 100 switchbacks back down past Howard Lake to High Bridge, then the shuttle road (or shuttle bus, if timed right) back to Stehekin Landing. If early-season snow still covers the upper talus/glacier shelf, some parties glissade short, low-angle snow sections with an ice axe for self-arrest rather than downclimbing rock, but there is no fixed rappel infrastructure on this route.
hazards: huge elevation gain from Stehekin valley (roughly 6,600 ft one-way to the summit)
Class 3 summit block above a trail, way-marked only by faded, intermittent red-arrow paint — route-finding is the main hazard, not the climbing
loose 'kitty litter' scree on slabs near exposed drop-offs on the summit ledges
fully remote approach with no road access to the trailhead itself (ferry/floatplane/trail only to Stehekin)
hot, dry, largely waterless lower trail — dehydration/heat risk on the switchbacks below Heaton Camp

waysIn.name: High Bridge and the McGregor Mountain Trail
waysIn.season: August into early September is the reliable window, once the talus and the shelf above the glacier have melted out. Carry an axe if snow still lies on either.
waysIn.notes: There is no road to the bottom of this one — Stehekin is reached by boat, floatplane or the long trail in, and from Stehekin Landing the valley road runs eleven miles up to its end at High Bridge, walkable, bikeable or by shuttle. From High Bridge the tread heads north on the old wagon grade and the Pacific Crest Trail, climbs steadily to Howard Lake, and reaches the signed McGregor Mountain junction a short way past the lake, just before the crest trail tips over and starts back downhill. Howard Lake is reliable water and a useful confirmation you are on route; if you are losing elevation you have walked past the junction. Above the junction the trail winds behind the lake, commits to one long switchback across a hot, dusty open slope, and then settles into a relentless grind — close to a hundred switchbacks up an open southwest-facing shoulder with essentially no shade. A seasonal falls off a short scramble path near the first big viewpoint is worth the detour, because water is scarce from there on. The trail crosses a clear creek, reaches the lower of two glacial cirques on rocky, sandy moraine, and ends at Heaton Camp just above the terminal moraine among larches, where a snowmelt stream a short way below camp is the last dependable water. Above camp another set of tight switchbacks ends at a rocky outcropping and the maintained trail simply stops.
hazards: roughly a vertical mile of gain from the valley floor with almost no shade and no dependable water below Heaton Camp
loose gravel on slab directly above significant exposure on the summit ledges — the descent is the more dangerous half
route-finding, not climbing difficulty, is the real crux above the trail's end
a snowfield and talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier that can hold firm snow into midsummer
no road access to the trailhead itself, so an injured party is a long way from help

name: West Ridge / Southwest Approach
approach: From the Goodell Creek (Upper Group Campground) trailhead just east of Goodell Creek Campground off SR-20 near Newhalem, pick up the unsigned climbers'-path (no trail number — this is a boot path, not a maintained Park trail) that starts behind a large boulder near the campground. There is reliable running water along the roadbed and at a stream crossing just before the steep climb begins, then none reliable again until Terror Basin, so top off bottles there. The path first follows the old Goodell Creek roadbed up the valley for about 4 miles at a gentle grade and is notorious for blowdown — expect to climb over or duck under dozens of downed logs. At a cairned turnoff near 1,700 ft it turns uphill and switchbacks through forest along a spur ridge south of Terror Creek; around 3,200 ft it gains the crest of the forested ridge, and the whole climb from the turnoff is a steady, unrelenting 4,000 ft of gain in about 2 miles. Near 4,000 ft it crosses a small talus field, circles left, and makes a rising traverse beneath a rock band at about 4,800 ft before kicking up a final steep gully. From there, heather benches and open slabs lead north for a couple of miles, with blueberries in late summer, to a notch in the ridge crest at roughly 6,200-6,350 ft — the high point of the approach. The north side of this notch is the crux of the approach, not the climb: in late-season/low-snow conditions it is steep, loose, chossy terrain for about 400 vertical feet (stay skier's-right — going straight down is a bad idea); early in the season it holds a firmer snow finger with a short, steeper headwall (reported up to ~80 degrees for the last 20-30 ft) that some parties rope up for or protect with a short lower. Below the notch, a small flat gravelly basin near 5,800 ft with running water is the standard Terror Basin camp. From camp, a long traverse over benches and granite slabs, trending slightly downhill, reaches a glacial lake outlet and then slabs below the Terror Glacier remnant; the glacier crossing is short and low-angle but can show bare ice by late summer — most parties cross unroped in stable conditions with crampons on. This leads to the base of the snow/rock gully that climbs to the 7,200 ft col between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan Spire, where the technical climbing begins. One-way distance from car to high camp is roughly 7-8 miles with 6,000+ ft of gain; a fit, loaded party should plan on 6-8+ hours.
descent: This route is descended by reversing the line of ascent essentially top to bottom — there is no separate walk-off. From the summit, downclimb the short, exposed Class 3 rock back down to the base of the summit block, then reverse the scree-and-heather ridge to the 7,200 ft Inspiration-McMillan col and descend the snow/rock gully below it, following the same snow finger climbed on the way up. That finger is glissade-able in soft, sun-affected afternoon snow, but if it is firm or icy (common in the morning or early season) parties often belay the downclimb or make a single short rappel/lower instead — one rope length is plenty (a single 30m section has been reported as sufficient), off natural anchors since there is nothing bolted or fixed on this route: a sling around a rock horn on the rock steps near the col, or a snow bollard/picket if the finger itself is icy. From the foot of the gully, recross the Terror Glacier remnant and the granite benches back toward Terror Basin, then climb back up the loose, chossy north-side gully to the ridge notch (the same skier's-right line used on the approach — avoid the direct fall line) and descend the heather benches on its far side toward the Goodell Creek drainage. From there it's a straightforward but long retrace of the forested trail, roughly 4 miles through the blowdown-choked lower section, back to the Goodell Creek trailhead. Total descent is on the order of 8,000-10,000 ft of elevation loss. The one rappel/protected-lower point is condition-dependent — more likely needed early season or in icy conditions on the snow finger or notch headwall — rather than a fixed technical rappel every party makes.
hazards: loose rock, especially in the rotten red gully skier's-right of the standard descent line
steep snow (up to ~40°) and a small crevasse/moat at the 7,200 ft Inspiration-McMillan col
exposed, lightly protected class 3 step just below the true summit
long, unmaintained approach with 100+ downed logs, washouts, and route-finding on an unofficial climber's trail
remoteness — no cell coverage, multi-day commitment, and a slow SAR response if something goes wrong
Terror Glacier crossing carries crevasse and glacier-travel hazard even though it is typically done unroped.
The summit ridge is narrow and heavily exposed, with large cliffs on both sides in places.
Rockfall and loose rock are recurring themes in trip reports of this route.
Weather can deteriorate quickly this deep in the Picket Range, complicating the long retreat.

waysIn.name: Goodell Creek climbers' path to the 6,200 ft notch and Terror Basin, then the Terror Glacier to the Inspiration-McMillan col gully
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Goodell Creek Upper Group Campground trailhead just east of Goodell Creek Campground off SR-20 near Newhalem, pick up the unsigned climbers' path that starts behind a large boulder near the campground. There is reliable running water along the roadbed and at a stream crossing just before the steep climb begins, and then none reliable again until Terror Basin.

The path first follows the old Goodell Creek roadbed up the valley for about 4 miles at a gentle grade and is notorious for blowdown; expect to climb over or duck under dozens of downed logs. At a cairned turnoff near 1,700 ft it turns uphill and switchbacks through forest along a spur ridge south of Terror Creek; around 3,200 ft it gains the crest of the forested ridge, and the whole climb from the turnoff is roughly 4,000 ft of gain in about 2 miles. Near 4,000 ft it crosses a small talus field, circles left, makes a rising traverse beneath a rock band at about 4,800 ft, then kicks up a final steep gully. Heather benches and open slabs then lead north for a couple of miles to a notch in the ridge crest at roughly 6,200-6,350 ft, the high point of the approach.

The north side of that notch is the crux of the approach, not of the climb: in late-season low-snow conditions it is steep, loose, chossy terrain for about 400 vertical feet, and you should stay skier's right rather than going straight down. Early season it holds a firmer snow finger with a short headwall reported up to about 80 degrees for the last 20-30 ft, which some parties rope up for. Below the notch, a small flat gravelly basin near 5,800 ft with running water is the standard Terror Basin camp.
hazards: Dozens of downed logs in the first couple of miles of the climbers' path
No reliable water between the foot of the steep climb and Terror Basin
400 ft of steep, loose choss on the north side of the 6,200 ft notch late season; stay skier's right
An early-season snow finger with a headwall reported to about 80 degrees at the notch
A moat at the top of the summit gully late season
Poor footing and rockfall onto a party strung out below on the scree ridge
Concentrated exposure in the last few moves between the false and true summits

name: South Route
approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead at the end of FR-6024 (Barclay Creek Road, ~2,280 ft), start up the maintained Barclay Lake Trail #1055 — an easy, well-graded path through old-growth forest paralleling Barclay Creek. After a little over a mile, a few hundred feet past the log bridge that crosses Barclay Creek (roughly 47.792, -121.459), leave the maintained trail; this is well before Barclay Lake itself. Cross toward the base of the south face and pick through brush and talus to locate a Y-shaped side drainage coming down off Merchant Peak (around 47.789, -121.436) — trip reports warn this creek mouth has become overgrown and is easy to walk past; look for a faint boot path of piled rocks leading 100–200 feet into the trees to pick up the creek bed proper. From there the 'trail' is the drainage itself: boulder-hop and scramble directly up the Merchant Creek gully, passing three main waterfall/rock steps. Waterfall 1 is bypassed on climbers-left via an established boot path; Waterfall 2 is passed by working right toward a cliff band and traversing over the top; Waterfall 3 is the crux of the entire approach — a jumble of large, jammed boulders and chockstones with small holds sitting on loose, sandy-mud rock, passed via a line on climbers-left. Above the falls the gully opens into brush, forest, and then heather meadows/slopes (the 'South Slope'); continue up onto the East Ridge for a final ~300 feet of solid, enjoyable Class 3 scrambling to the 6,113 ft summit. Water is available from Barclay Creek at the trailhead and from Merchant Creek throughout the gully (treat before drinking). Hazards include loose rock and rockfall exposure in the gully (helmet strongly recommended, especially with other parties above/below), real route-finding difficulty locating the correct side drainage, the exposed, loose Class 3 moves at Waterfall 3, and lingering snow/avalanche debris in the gully into early summer. Trip reports log roughly 3–4 hours from trailhead to summit.
descent: Because this is a scramble rather than a technical rock route, there is no separate rappel-descent line or walk-off trail — nearly all parties reverse the ascent gully (East Ridge to South Slope to South Gully) back down to Barclay Creek and out the Barclay Lake Trail. The crux of the descent is getting back down through the Waterfall 3 chockstone/boulder jam: most parties downclimb it facing in on climbers-left, on the same loose, sandy-mud rock and small holds used on the way up. Some parties choose to rappel this one step instead, particularly in wet conditions or with a less experienced group — trip reports document a single rappel here using a fixed rappel ring at the top of the falls (visible in trip-report photos), backed up with a natural anchor (one party used a nearby log) and the rope run through the ring; a single-strand rappel off a 30m or a doubled 60m rope is more than enough length to clear the drop. Treat that ring as unverified, aged fixed gear rather than a bolted sport anchor, and back it up with your own natural anchor (tree, log, or boulder) if you have any doubt about its condition. Below Waterfall 3, downclimb/scramble past Waterfalls 2 and 1 as ascended, relocate the faint boot path back to the side-drainage junction, and follow it back to the Barclay Lake Trail bridge and out to the trailhead. Descent-specific hazards: rockfall risk is higher going down than up since parties above kick debris onto those below (stay tight as a group or descend one at a time through the gully), the rock in the falls sections gets slick when wet, and it's easy to drop into the wrong side-gully lower down if you don't backtrack carefully to the same drainage used on ascent. Round trip is commonly reported around 6.5–7 hours car-to-car, with the descent taking nearly as long as the ascent (one trip report logged 3.7 hours up and 2.5 hours down).
hazards: steep brush and route-finding on the lower approach and where the boot path leaves Barclay Lake Trail
loose rock throughout the gully, worst at the crux waterfall (~3,700 ft) where small holds sit in sandy mud
exposed class 3 chockstone/chimney at the third waterfall
lingering wet snowfields and avalanche potential in the gully into June
flash-flood/high-water risk in the creek gully after heavy rain
rockfall from other parties above in the narrow gully

waysIn.name: Barclay Lake Trail to the Y-shaped drainage
waysIn.season: July to September
waysIn.notes: Start up the maintained Barclay Lake Trail through old-growth beside the creek — easy, well-graded walking. You leave it after a little over a mile, a few hundred feet past the log bridge over Barclay Creek and well before the lake, then pick through brush and talus toward the base of the south face to find the drainage. From there the drainage IS the route: boulder-hop and scramble straight up the creek bed past three waterfall steps into brush, forest and then upper heather meadows. Water runs in the gully most of the season; treat it before drinking.
hazards: Loose, sandy granodiorite throughout the gully, worst at the crux waterfall
Rockfall from parties above in a narrow drainage
An exposed chockstone squeeze at the third waterfall
Wet snowfields and avalanche debris in the gully into June
High water in the creek bed after heavy rain

name: Milk n' Honey
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) — 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, forest along Mountaineer Creek with a log-bridge crossing at 1.5 miles, bearing left at the Lake Stuart Trail junction, finishing on a boulder moraine to the outlet (2.5-3 hours). Fill water here, the last source. Follow the trail along the lake's west shore to its southeast end and take the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail up steep talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min; holds wet snow into July), then break climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully system below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Milk n' Honey (5.11) sits in the same general wall area as The Scoop and Rikki Tikki Tavi, toward the right side of the formation; expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final scramble to the base. Figure 3.5-4 hours car-to-base.
descent: Milk n' Honey tops out on Colchuck Balanced Rock's upper wall and, like its neighbors, most likely shares the standard summit descent: class 3-4 scrambling around the right side of the true summit block to a sandy scree/talus gully, descended clockwise back around the peak to the base of the climbs (45 min-1hr), with a short step near the top sometimes eased by an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn (natural anchor) on the east side. No full rappel of the route is confirmed to be required.
hazards: Rockfall potential on approach and lower pitches

name: East Face / East Buttress
approach: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road (Forest Road 15), elevation ~3,600 ft. Follow the Cascade Pass Trail (a well-graded, switchbacking National Park trail, unnumbered but universally called the Cascade Pass Trail) 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft of gain to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft) — a broad, scenic saddle with no reliable water beyond seasonal snowmelt, so top off at a creek crossing lower on the trail. From the pass, do not continue on the maintained Pacific Crest/Stehekin trail; instead pick up a climbers' path on the right (south) side that bends SSE and makes a rising traverse across the heather-and-talus flanks of Mixup Arm and Mixup Peak's east slopes at roughly the 6,000 ft contour. This traverse crosses a minor spur ridge and several steep snow gullies that hold snow well into summer — in early season these have poor runout above a roughly 400 ft drop, so an ice axe and comfort with a traverse on firm snow are important; a slip here has real consequences. Continue traversing to the toe of the Cache Glacier (~6,000-6,200 ft), then ascend moderate glaciated/snow slopes (watch for crevasses in early-mid season) aiming for the obvious notch system below and left of Mixup's summit — commonly called the 'V-notch' — just north of Gunsight Notch, the main portal between Mixup, the Triplets, and Cascade Peak. Gain the notch/saddle via a short snow or scree gully, then work up class 3-4 ramps on the east side to a feature climbers call the 'White Staircase' (exposed class 3), which leads to a point roughly 100 ft below the summit where the roped mid-5th-class pitches of the East Face/East Buttress begin. Camping is prohibited at Cascade Pass itself and on Mixup Arm, so parties either push the whole approach and climb as one very long car-to-car day (7-9 hours to the summit alone), or continue past the notch/Cache Col area to established sites at Kool-Aid Lake (~6,120 ft) or near Cache Col for a lower-effort summit day. Rockfall — both natural and climber-triggered — is a real hazard on the upper approach gullies and staircase; keep parties tight and helmets on well before roping up.
descent: Descend by reversing the final scramble pitches/downclimbing back to the top of the technical face (the uppermost section is a downclimb/scramble to the top of the East Face), then begin a rappel sequence rather than trying to downclimb the buttress itself — the rock is loose enough that down-climbing the route is not recommended. From a small ledge/anchor on the east side just below the summit, a 50 m rappel gets you down the steepest upper wall (rockfall-prone — the next rappeller should move off to the side immediately, not straight down, to avoid anyone above). Below that, from the bottom of the shoulder, one rappel on a single 60 m rope reaches the belay station at the top of the second climbing pitch. From there the line drops over an overhanging section to just below the north side of Gunsight Notch: one double-rope rappel with two ropes, or two rappels on a single 60 m rope. That is four rappels on one 60 m rope, which is what parties report, or three with two ropes. Anchors are fixed natural slings and cord rather than bolts, and parties regularly add cord or rebuild one, so carry some. Move off the fall line as soon as you are down each rappel; rockfall knocked loose by the party above is a recognized hazard here. Below the notch, re-descend the glacier and snowfield and Mixup Arm to Cascade Pass.
hazards: rockfall in the approach gullies and at the notches — described as a serious hazard on both ascent and descent in multiple trip reports
moat at Gunsight Notch, which widens through the season and can force mid-5th-class climbing on loose, dirty rock to exit it
crevasse hazard crossing the small glacier/snowfield below the East Face
lingering snow on ledges into July/August in heavy-snow years
summit and ridge exposure with limited protection on the final class-4/5 moves ('Class 5 climbing, but no place to place pro, so you pretend it's Class 4')

waysIn.name: Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm bench and the Cache Glacier
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; access gets harder through August as the Cache Glacier recedes
waysIn.notes:
Cascade River Road runs about 22-23 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead at 3,600 ft. Follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to the pass at roughly 5,400 ft. There is no reliable water at the pass beyond seasonal snowmelt, so fill at a creek crossing lower down.

At the pass, near the benches, turn right (south) onto the obvious climbers' path — do not continue on the maintained trail toward Stehekin. The path bends south-southeast and makes a rising traverse across heather and talus on the flanks of Mixup Arm and Mixup Peak's east slopes at roughly the 6,000 ft contour, crossing a minor spur ridge.

This traverse crosses steep snow gullies that hold snow well into summer. In early season the runout is bad — a slip has a drop of several hundred feet below it — so an ice axe and genuine comfort on firm snow traverses are the entry requirement, not optional extras.

Continue to the toe of the Cache Glacier at about 6,000-6,200 ft. The described landmark is a seasonal waterfall: walk past it, turn right, and ascend the lobe of the Cache.

Camping is prohibited at Cascade Pass and on Mixup Arm, so this is either a long car-to-car day of 7-9 hours to the summit, or you continue past the notch to established sites at Kool-Aid Lake (about 6,120 ft) or near Cache Col.
hazards: Steep snow gullies on the traverse with a bad runout in early season
Wrong notch — U-notch on the left versus V-notch on the right
Bergschrunds flanking the snow tongue, ten to fifteen feet down to rock
Rockfall, natural and climber-triggered, on the upper gullies and staircase
Moat at the glacier-rock junction, worsening through the season and year on year
No camping permitted at Cascade Pass or on Mixup Arm

name: North Col
approach: From the Barlow Pass Trailhead (end of the paved Mountain Loop Highway drive), the approach is in two clearly different stages before you ever leave a maintained tread. Stage one is 4 flat, easy miles up the gated, washed-out Monte Cristo Road along the South Fork Sauk River to the Monte Cristo ghost town (~2,800 ft) — a couple of cable/suspension bridges cross the river en route, and this stretch is runnable/bikeable in dry conditions. At the townsite, walk past the old cabins, cross the bridge over 76 Creek, and follow "Dumas Street" through the settlement to pick up signed Glacier Basin Trail #719. Stage two is the real climb: the first half-mile follows an old mining road grade along Glacier Creek, then the trail turns into slick rock scrambling more than hiking — steep, eroded, hands-on-rock terrain climbing past Glacier Falls, with numerous cascades and slick, root-braided rock steps that are notably harder (and slicker) descending than ascending. The trail crosses into Henry M. Jackson Wilderness and skirts the northeast edge of Mystery Hill before leveling out into Glacier Basin (~4,500 ft) after about 2.5 miles and ~1,700 ft of gain from Monte Cristo — roughly 6.5 miles and ~2,100 ft from the car. Glacier Creek parallels the whole climb and is a reliable water source, but it drains historic mine workings — treat/filter and be aware of elevated arsenic/heavy-metal readings noted by the Forest Service, especially in the lower reaches near the old townsite. From Glacier Basin the maintained trail ends; leave it and climb open talus and (typically) persistent steep snow — up to ~45° for a few hundred vertical feet — directly toward the obvious North Col (~6,760+ ft) on Monte Cristo's north ridge, with the Wilmans Peaks and Wilmans Glacier looming close overhead to climber's right. An ice axe and comfort on steep firm snow are essentially mandatory into midsummer; a moat can open at the col and the step across it can be intimidating or, late season, impassable. From the North Col, contour south (skier's/climber's left) across snow or talus below the summit cliffs, scouting for the obvious break/gully in the rock that gives the easiest way up to the base of the short summit chimney.
descent: Descent reverses the ascent line (the North Col Route is a there-and-back, not a loop). From the summit, downclimb the ~100 ft of Class 3 terrain back to the top of the short chimney. The chimney itself is the technical crux both ways — about 30 ft requiring three moves of exposed climbing (roughly 5.6, 5.2, 5.6) — and most parties rappel it rather than downclimb, especially with a second climber or in the wet/mossy conditions common on this shaded north-facing rock. A fixed/bolted rappel anchor (reported as a single new-ish bolt backed up by a natural nut placement) sits a short distance below the chimney; a single 60m rope is sufficient to reach easier ground. Treat the bolt+nut anchor with normal backcountry skepticism — inspect it, and carry a nut or small cam to supplement or replace it if it looks worn, since this is a lightly-traveled scramble route without the anchor redundancy of a popular sport crag. Below the rappel, continue down and contour north back to the North Col, re-cross the moat/schrund, and descend the steep snow slope (glissade only if you can self-arrest reliably; it firms up fast in the afternoon shade) back down to the talus and into Glacier Basin. From there it's a plain hike out: reverse Trail #719 down through the slick-rock section above Glacier Falls (use extra caution here — this is the section trip reports flag as harder and more slip-prone descending than climbing), back through Monte Cristo townsite, and out the 4 miles of old road to Barlow Pass. Helmets are recommended for the entire upper mountain (col to summit) given loose rock in the chimney/gully and any parties above.
hazards: short but unavoidable 5.6 rock chimney — a roped technical pitch, not a Class 3 scramble move
steep snow (reported to ~45°) on the North Col approach — solid self-arrest/crampon skills required
moat gap at the base of the chimney can open by mid-to-late summer, blocking or seriously complicating access
loose, blocky rock in the gully and on the descent, worsened by parties above
long, multi-stage approach (bike/hike + closed road + trail + off-trail talus/snow) with washed-out river crossings and no cell coverage in the basin
routefinding among the cluster of peaks — easy to drift onto Cadet or Kyes terrain by mistake
afternoon thunderstorms building over the exposed upper peak

waysIn.name: Barlow Pass, the closed road and Glacier Basin
waysIn.season: June is the classic window: enough snow remains on the col talus to speed travel while the moat at the chimney's base is usually still closed. By late July the moat can open and block or seriously complicate access, and the talus turns loose and tedious once melted out.
waysIn.notes: Two clearly different stages before you leave maintained tread. From the gate at Barlow Pass the old Monte Cristo road runs four flat miles along the South Fork Sauk to the ghost town, crossing the river on cable and suspension bridges; the grade is easy and rideable in dry conditions, though road and bridge washouts mean most parties on bikes walk them through a short section or two. At the townsite, walk past the old cabins, cross the bridge over 76 Creek and follow the street through the settlement to pick up signed Glacier Basin Trail #719. The first half mile is an old mining road grade along Glacier Creek; then the tread turns steep, eroded and hands-on-rock, climbing past Glacier Falls on slick, root-braided rock steps that are considerably harder and more slip-prone descending than ascending. The trail crosses into wilderness, skirts the northeast edge of Mystery Hill and levels into Glacier Basin. Glacier Creek is reliable water the whole way but drains historic mine workings and carries elevated arsenic and heavy metals, worst low down near the townsite — treat it. The maintained trail ends at the basin; from there open talus and persistent steep snow, up to about forty-five degrees for a few hundred vertical feet, lead up the centre gully to the obvious col on the north ridge, with the Wilmans Peaks close overhead on the right.
hazards: a short but unavoidable roped rock chimney — this is not a Class 3 scramble move
steep firm snow to around forty-five degrees on the col approach, needing an axe and reliable self-arrest into midsummer
the moat at the base of the chimney, which can open by mid-to-late summer and add rock climbing or block access outright
loose red volcanic breccia above the chimney, worst in the final two hundred feet, with rockfall onto anyone below
washed-out river crossings on the closed road and no cell coverage in the basin
drifting onto neighbouring Cadet or Kyes terrain among the cluster of peaks
afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed upper mountain

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Four approaches reach Monument Peak, all long and remote — this is deep in the Pasayten Wilderness near the Canadian border, and most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with a high camp. The most common is via the Monument Creek Trailhead on Lost River Road/FR 5400 (about 22 miles northwest of Winthrop via Mazama), starting at roughly 2,400 ft. From the trailhead, follow Monument Creek Trail No. 484 up the Lost River valley; the first ~4 miles are well-maintained through old-growth forest and along rock slopes to the Eureka Creek confluence (Eureka Falls Camp) — this is your last easy, reliable water before a long dry stretch. Beyond Eureka Creek the trail has been essentially unmaintained for 25+ years, brushy and choked with deadfall, and route-finding becomes real work. Ford Eureka Creek (can run thigh-to-waist deep during snowmelt — a genuine early-summer hazard) then pick up the abandoned tread climbing onto Pistol Ridge, following it up to 7,100-ft Pistol Pass around mile 11. From the pass, descend about a mile on the trail, finishing on a short spur, to Lake of the Woods in the Monument–Lake Mountain basin, a common high camp — about 12 miles and 5,300 ft of gain from the trailhead. From camp, traverse cross-country northwest to the ~7,400-ft saddle below Lake Mountain, then descend into Lower Monument Basin (~6,100 ft); the lake-outlet creek here is your last dependable water for the summit push and can shrink to a trickle late in the season. From the basin, climb a left-angling ramp system to gain Monument Peak's south/southeast ridge at about 6,900 ft, then follow a long talus traverse toward the summit. The final section involves roughly a half-pitch of Class 3 (locally Class 3-4) scrambling where the ridge merges with the southeast slopes, sometimes complicated by a steep snowfield just below the true summit that can still require an ice axe (or a class 3/4 rock detour around its left side) into midsummer. Three alternative approaches exist: dropping in from 6,960-ft Slate Pass on the Harts Pass Road down to the Robinson Creek Trail No. 478 and Ferguson Lake Trail No. 474A (reportedly the easiest, though not shortest, reaching the same basin from the north); via the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead just past Harts Pass on Trail No. 498, crossing the Middle Fork Pasayten River and picking up Robinson Creek Trail No. 478 then Ferguson Lake Trail No. 474A; or a longer approach from the Lost Creek/Monument Creek trailhead side. Whichever line is used, expect long, remote travel with significant off-trail brush and route-finding on the final miles — carry a map/GPS and budget extra time.
descent: This is a walk-off — there is no rappelling on the standard scramble route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 3 (occasionally 3-4) rock/talus off the summit block to regain the south/southeast ridge at roughly 6,900 ft, then descend the left-angling ramp system back into Lower Monument Basin, topping off water at the lake-outlet creek if needed, before climbing back up to the Lake Mountain saddle (~7,400 ft) and dropping to high camp at Lake of the Woods. Where a summit snowfield was crossed on the ascent, most parties recross it on foot (or skirt around its left side on rock) rather than glissade, since it can remain firm or icy well into summer. The main descent hazards are loose talus, exposed Class 3 scrambling near the summit, and route-finding fatigue — several parties describe finishing the final talus slopes back to camp by headlamp. No fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel gear are used on this route. From camp, retrace whichever approach trail was used — Pistol Pass and the Eureka Creek ford back to the Monument Creek Trailhead, or the Ferguson Lake/Robinson Creek trail back to Slate Pass or the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead — to reach the road.
hazards: loose, blocky talus on the upper mountain
long, remote, multi-day Pasayten approach with no cell service and slow rescue response
Eureka Creek ford (cold, and can run high with early-season snowmelt)
faint/unmaintained tread beyond Pistol Pass — real route-finding difficulty, especially on the return
lingering snowfields near the summit into early summer that can require crampons/ice axe
afternoon thunderstorms are common in this rain-shadow, east-slopes climate
exposed Class 3 (occasionally harder) moves on the final summit block

waysIn.name: Lower Monument Basin and the left-angling ramp
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Monument is the most rugged thing in this group and sits nearly as an island, with Eureka Creek wrapping three sides of it. The travelled approach is the Monument Creek trail from the Lost River road: well maintained through old growth for about four miles to the Eureka Creek confluence, then unmaintained, brushy and deadfall-choked, with a ford of Eureka Creek that can run thigh to waist deep in early summer. From there the abandoned tread climbs onto Pistol Ridge and over Pistol Pass, and most parties camp near Lake of the Woods. Summit day is long enough that finishing the last talus by headlamp is common.
hazards: Loose blocky talus on the whole upper mountain
Exposed scrambling on the final summit block, Class 3 or harder
Snowfield below the summit that can hold firm or icy into midsummer
Eureka Creek ford, cold and high with early-season snowmelt
Faint, unmaintained tread beyond Pistol Pass, worse on the return
Long, remote, multi-day approach with no cell service
Afternoon thunderstorms common in this rain-shadow climate

waysIn.name: From Slate Pass by Robinson Creek and the Ferguson Lake trail
waysIn.notes: Gentler, though not shorter. Drop north from Slate Pass to the Robinson Creek trail along the Middle Fork Pasayten, then near the big meadow horse camp take the Ferguson Lake trail, which descends about seven miles to Eureka Creek just south of the peak. From there, pick a line up the south side or into the basin between Monument and Lake Mountain. Three approaches off Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge use the Ferguson Lake trail and reach the same basin from the north.
hazards: Long approach via Slate Pass, the Robinson Creek trail and the Ferguson Lake trail to Eureka Creek, remote with no cell service
Eureka Creek crossing near the peak, cold and high in early-season melt
Loose blocky talus on the upper mountain
Exposed scrambling on the final summit block
Snowfield below the summit into midsummer
Afternoon thunderstorms common in this climate
waysIn.whyThisWay: When coming from the Harts Pass side to avoid the brushy, unmaintained Monument Creek trail and the Eureka Creek ford; an easier walk but not shorter, usually a two-day trip.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FR-4065 off the Mountain Loop Highway), follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (Trail #707) about half a mile. Just before the trail crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish River, leave it for a faint abandoned path on the river's east side, or take the line of least resistance along that side. The path soon fades into slide alder, brush and rock debris; fording the river to dodge the brush is hazardous in high runoff, especially in late spring and early summer. Work up the valley past a house-sized boulder near 3,100 ft, then either cross the river and climb a ridge ramp southwest to the upper basin (about 4,000 ft), or continue to a broad basin at about 3,700 ft and climb the steep gully (or the slabs to its right) directly east of it, leaving it to the right where that is easy. Climb snow-covered slabs to a notch in Morning Star's southeast ridge at about 5,600 ft; these slabs are the route's main avalanche concern. The round trip is roughly 5.5-6 miles with 3,700-4,200 ft of gain. The steep gully is often icy when snow-filled, so helmet, ice axe and crampons are standard early in the season; early-season snow makes this a basic alpine climb rather than a scramble.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — reverse the ascent line, there is no rappelling on the standard route (0 rappels). From the 6,020 ft summit, descend on or near the south ridge to the broad gully, downclimb it into the southeast basin, traverse back below the cliffs and climb about 200 ft through trees to the notch in the southeast ridge. The gully (icy in early/mid-season) is often easier to face in and downclimb than to descend facing out, and crampons make the icy sections much smoother; groups should stay tight and avoid stacking directly above one another. From the notch, descend the snow-covered slabs (watch for avalanche conditions) and the gully or ridge ramp back into the South Fork Stillaguamish valley, then retrace the brushy east-side path to the Sunrise Mine Trail and the trailhead.
hazards: avalanche danger on the steep snow-covered slabs below the southeast-ridge notch — the route's main avalanche concern
fording the South Fork Stillaguamish, whether to dodge the brush or on the option that crosses near the 3,100 ft boulder, is unsafe in high runoff
lingering steep snow in the gullies and on the slabs into early summer, often icy near the notch and in the ~45° gully to the south ridge
thick brush, slide alder and hard avalanche debris along the east side of the South Fork Stillaguamish, with a path that comes and goes
exposure on the final summit scramble moves

waysIn.name: South Fork Stillaguamish valley
waysIn.season: July to September. Earlier, snow on the slabs and in the gullies makes it a basic alpine climb, and an ice axe and crampons are standard until it has gone.
waysIn.notes: From the Sunrise Mine trailhead, follow the trail about half a mile. Just before it crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish, leave it for a faint path up the river's east side; it comes and goes and soon disappears into slide alder, brush and avalanche debris. Past a house-sized boulder near 3,000-3,100 ft, either cross the river and climb a ridge ramp southwest to the upper basin near 4,000 ft, or continue to the broad basin at about 3,700 ft and turn sharply up the steep gully directly east (or the slabs to its right). Snow-covered slabs then lead to the notch in the southeast ridge at about 5,600 ft.
hazards: Thick brush, slide alder and hard avalanche debris along the east side of the river
Fording the river to dodge the brush is unsafe in high runoff
The snow-covered slabs below the notch are the route's main avalanche concern
The ~45° gully from the southeast basin to the south ridge is often icy when snow-filled

name: Avalanche-White Salmon Glaciers
approach: Start at the Cold Springs trailhead (about 5,600 ft) at the end of FR 8040 and walk the South Climb Trail up the old roadbed to its junction with the Round the Mountain Trail near 6,200 ft. Turn right (northwest) onto the Round the Mountain Trail and follow its up-and-down traverse for roughly two miles, much of it under snow in early season, to the stream draining the Avalanche Glacier basin near 6,100 ft. Follow the stream and the moraines above it to the moraine-filled bowl at about 7,200 ft, where the Avalanche Glacier route and the Southwest Chutes meet. The glacier begins above this bowl, and a camp here shortens the summit day.
descent: Climb out onto the summit plateau and head for the true summit, then descend the South Spur: cross the crater rim past Pikers Peak and follow the broad snow slopes of Crescent Ridge down to the Lunch Counter flats, where glissading is common on soft snow. From there the South Climb Trail runs down the old roadbed to Cold Springs, so no shuttle is needed if you started there. Going back down the White Salmon and Avalanche Glaciers is possible in good snow but means a short, steep 45-degree entry below the summit saddle and crevasses that open on the northern and western parts of the glacier by midsummer. Carry an axe and rope team for either descent.

name: Lava Glacier Headwall
approach: Same trailhead and trail as the Lyman Glacier approach: Killen Creek Trail #113 from the Killen Creek Trailhead, about 3.1 miles through lodgepole forest (crossing East Fork Adams Creek near mile 2.5) to the PCT at ~6,100 ft, then the High Camp Trail #10 another 1.0 mile to High Camp/Adams Glacier Meadows (~6,900 ft). From High Camp, the Lava Glacier Headwall is reached more directly than Lyman: traverse off-trail across the lava fields toward the toe of the Lava Glacier without needing to work around Lava Ridge, reaching the base of the headwall (the triangular ice/snow face bounded by the North Ridge on one side and Lava Ridge on the other). This is glacial/talus terrain with crevasse hazard on the glacier itself. Sources consistently stress climbing this face early season — late spring to early summer — since it becomes icy and rockfall-prone as the snowpack recedes later in summer.
descent: Descend the North Ridge back toward High Camp, the same non-technical but tedious scree/boulder walk-off used for the Adams Glacier and Lyman Glacier routes on this side of the mountain — long, loose volcanic scree, some narrow/exposed sections, and rockfall risk onto other parties, but no rappelling required on the standard line. From High Camp, retrace the High Camp Trail and Killen Creek Trail to the trailhead. The alternative is to continue over the summit and descend the South Climb route to Cold Springs, which lands you at a different trailhead and requires a shuttle.
hazards: Steep ice/snow headwall with serac hazard
Crevasse navigation on the Lava Glacier
Rockfall as the headwall warms

waysIn.name: Killen Creek, the PCT and High Camp, then across the lava fields to the Lava Glacier
waysIn.season: Roughly May-Jun. This is a cold-season face: it turns icy and starts shedding rock as the snowpack recedes later in summer
waysIn.notes:
From the Killen Creek trailhead on the forest road near Takhlakh Lake at about 4,600 ft, follow Killen Creek Trail #113 roughly 3.1 miles through open lodgepole forest, crossing East Fork Adams Creek near mile 2.5, to the PCT at about 6,100 ft. Cross the PCT onto the High Camp Trail #10 for another mile to High Camp at Adams Creek Meadows, about 6,900 ft, on the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine.

From High Camp this route is reached more directly than the Lyman: traverse off-trail east across the lava fields to the toe of the Lava Glacier, without needing to work around Lava Ridge.

The approach roads are gravel and seasonal, opening as snow clears.
hazards: Steep ice and snow with serac hazard on a face that must be climbed continuously
Rockfall increasing sharply as the headwall warms
Crevasse navigation on the Lava Glacier apron
A long descent of the North Ridge on loose volcanic scree with rockfall onto parties below
Seasonal gravel road access that opens late in a heavy year

name: Lyman Glacier
approach: From the Killen Creek Trailhead (FS Rd 2329, ~3 miles from Takhlakh Lake), follow Killen Creek Trail #113 through open, dusty lodgepole forest. Around 2.5 miles in you cross East Fork Adams Creek and its meadows (last reliable easy water before the high basin), then the trees thin as the trail climbs rockier terrain to meet the PCT (Trail #2000) at roughly 6,100 ft, about 3.1 miles from the trailhead. Continue straight across the PCT onto the High Camp Trail #10 for about 1.0 mile to High Camp / Adams Glacier Meadows at the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine (~6,900 ft) — a common base camp. From High Camp the route leaves maintained trail: traverse east/southeast, off-trail across lava fields and around or over the toe of Lava Ridge, crossing the toe of the Lava Glacier, to reach the base of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft. This traverse is glacier/talus travel with real route-finding, especially in low-snow years — a rope and crevasse-rescue gear are standard once on glacier ice. The Lyman Glacier itself splits around a rock outcrop; the north lobe (original route) and south lobe (40° lower half on unbroken neve/ice, upper half broken by crevasses and serac walls) both lead to a crux chute near 10,000 ft that varies 45–65° for about 50 ft depending on the year, then easier snow to the summit plateau.
descent: Standard descent is the North Ridge (also called the North Cleaver) or the adjacent snowfield beside it, dropping back toward High Camp — this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. It is the least pleasant part of the trip: long stretches of loose, rotten volcanic scree and boulders, occasional narrow/exposed sections, and a real chance of rockfall onto parties below, so groups should spread out and move quickly through the worst of it. No fixed anchors or rappels are used on the standard line; a short rope-assisted downclimb over an isolated rock band is occasionally used by parties uncomfortable with exposure, but this is improvised, not a bolted or standard rappel. Once back at High Camp, retrace the High Camp Trail and Killen Creek Trail to the trailhead. Some parties instead descend the South Climb route to the Cold Springs trailhead, which requires a car shuttle or a long road walk back to Killen Creek since it's a different trailhead entirely.
hazards: Crevasse and serac navigation on the Lyman Glacier
A short, steep crux chute at ~10,000 ft, reported anywhere from 45° to 65° over about 50 ft depending on the year — its difficulty varies significantly season to season
Long, sustained high-altitude climbing

waysIn.name: Killen Creek and High Camp, then east past Lava Ridge to the Lyman at 8,000 ft
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Jul; climbed in late spring and early summer as moderate to steep snow and sometimes alpine ice
waysIn.notes:
From the Killen Creek trailhead, follow Trail #113 through open dusty lodgepole forest. Around 2.5 miles you cross East Fork Adams Creek and its meadows — the last easy water before the high basin. The trees thin as the trail climbs rockier ground to the PCT at about 6,100 ft, roughly 3.1 miles in. Continue straight across onto High Camp Trail #10 for about a mile to High Camp at Adams Creek Meadows, near 6,900 ft.

From High Camp the maintained trail is done. Traverse east and southeast off-trail across lava fields, across the toe of the Lava Glacier and around or over the toe of Lava Ridge, to the base of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft. This is glacier and talus travel with real route-finding, worst in a low-snow year; rope and crevasse-rescue gear are standard once on ice.

Most of the route can be simul-climbed with a running belay on pickets. The standard descent is the North Ridge, not a reversal — long, loose volcanic scree, occasionally narrow, with a real chance of knocking rock onto parties below.
hazards: Crevasse and serac navigation on the Lyman, particularly on the south lobe's upper half
A short steep crux chute near 10,000 ft that varies from 45 to 65 degrees year to year
Long sustained high-altitude climbing with a late-season low-snow route-finding problem on the traverse
A descent down the North Ridge on loose rotten volcanic scree, with rockfall onto parties below
Seasonal gravel road access

name: North Ridge
approach: Killen Creek Trailhead (Trail #113, off FR 2329 via FR 23) climbs through forest and meadow ~3.1 mi/1,400 ft to the PCT, then continues to High Camp — roughly 4 mi and 2,300 ft of gain total from the trailhead — the shared base camp for the North Ridge, Adams Glacier, and Northwest Ridge routes. A common early start is to camp the night before on the Killen Creek Trail near 6,050 ft, just before the Pacific Crest Trail junction, then leave around 4 am and pass High Camp in the dark.
descent: Most parties descend the route itself, back down the North Ridge toward high camp; it is non-technical, mostly Class 2 over loose volcanic scree. Some parties instead carry over and descend the South Climb to Cold Springs, which requires a long car shuttle. Watch crevasses on any glacier descent. On the way down in early July, staying on the crest line, which cairns mark, is easier than dropping onto the side snow.
hazards: Steep, sustained snow on the upper ridge with rockfall from the ridge crest
Crevasses on the Adams and Lava glaciers either side of the ridge
Cornices on the ridgeline
Remote north-side approach — long self-reliant day

waysIn.name: Killen Creek trailhead and High Camp
waysIn.season: June through September; a snow route early, a loose rock route once it melts out
waysIn.notes:
The same walk in as the Adams Glacier and the Northwest Ridge, and High Camp is the shared base for all three. Killen Creek Trail #113 from the trailhead (~4,600 ft) runs about 3.1 miles to the PCT junction at roughly 6,100 ft; cross straight over onto High Camp Trail #10 for another mile to its end at about 6,900 ft on the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine. Camping is spread between 7,000 and 7,600 ft, including a glacial lake camp near 7,650 ft.

Access is by FR 23, 21 and 2329; FR 2329 is gravel and holds snow into early summer. East Fork Adams Creek, crossed about 2.5 miles up the trail, is the last dependable water.

Permits: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead, plus a Cascade Volcano Pass for travel above 7,000 ft in the summer season.

This is a longer and more committing day than the South Climb from a much quieter side of the mountain, and crevassed glacier lies on both flanks of the ridge and on the summit ice cap, so glacier skills are expected, unlike the South Spur.
hazards: Very loose volcanic rock the length of the ridge — helmets, and spacing between climbers
Crevassed glacier on both flanks if you leave the crest
Exposed snow travel between rock sections
Thin moraine tread above treeline, easy to lose in dark or whiteout
No running water above East Fork Adams Creek

name: South Climb (South Spur)
approach: From Trout Lake, drive north on Mt Adams Rd to the Forest Road 23 junction; bear right about a mile to the signed FR 80 junction for South Climb, turn left and follow FR 80 for 3.7 miles to FR 8040, then follow FR 8040 (steep, narrow, sharp switchbacks — no RVs/trailers) for 8.1 miles to its end at the South Climb/Cold Springs trailhead (5,600 ft). The trail follows an old roadbed through the burn scar, enters subalpine forest and meadows, crosses Round-the-Mountain Trail #9 and the PCT, then climbs Crescent Ridge to the base of the summit snowfields.
descent: Retrace the ascent line: cross back over the shallow summit crater, down over Piker's Peak, and descend the broad snow slopes of Suksdorf/Crescent Ridge to Lunch Counter, then follow the old roadbed back to the trailhead. Glissading is common on the lower snowfields in firm-but-soft conditions; watch for exposed rock and runout hazards in late season as snow recedes.
hazards: Whiteout navigation on the featureless upper snow slopes
Afternoon thunderstorms/rapid weather changes
Exposed, featureless slopes offer no shelter from lightning or wind.
Glissade chutes can turn to hard ice by midday, causing falls.

waysIn.name: Cold Springs trailhead and the Lunch Counter
waysIn.season: Late May through September; earlier in the season the whole route is a snow climb from the parking lot
waysIn.notes:
From Trout Lake, drive north on Mt Adams Road to the Forest Road 23 junction, bear right about a mile to the signed FR 80 turn for South Climb, then FR 80 for 3.7 miles to FR 8040, and FR 8040 for 8.1 miles — steep, narrow, sharp switchbacks, no RVs or trailers — to the South Climb / Cold Springs trailhead at 5,600 ft.

Permits: a Cascade Volcano Pass is required to travel above 7,000 ft in the Mount Adams Wilderness during the summer season (May 1 to September 30), and a free wilderness permit is needed for the trailhead. The wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead; the climbing pass is a single-trip pass sold only online, so buy and print it before driving up.

The trail begins on an old roadbed through burn scar, enters subalpine forest and meadow, crosses the Round-the-Mountain Trail and the PCT, then climbs Crescent Ridge toward the snowfields. In early season there is often no trail at all — just a snow slope leading out of the parking lot. Above the Crescent Glacier the way is meandering snowfields to the Lunch Counter.

The Lunch Counter (roughly 9,250–9,400 ft) is the standard camp: a broad rocky bench with hand-built rock windbreaks. Water is snowmelt. This is a route where the crowd itself is a factor — it is the most-climbed line on the mountain and the bench fills on summer weekends.
hazards: Rockfall and soft-snow postholing on the Crescent Glacier slopes in warm afternoons
Whiteout on the featureless snowfields between Crescent Glacier and the Lunch Counter
Turning around at Piker's Peak believing it is the summit
Uncontrolled glissading — the standard descent line has caused injuries
No water above the Lunch Counter; snowmelt only
Sharp switchbacks and rough surface on FR 8040, and snow blocking it early in the season

name: Wilson Glacier Headwall
approach: The Wilson Glacier sits on the east side of Mount Adams, descending from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft — a less-visited, less-documented flank than the standard south or north-side routes. Parties reach it via the Cold Springs/South Climb trailhead (5,600 ft, FS Rd 8040 off FS Rd 80): follow the South Climb Trail #183 about 1 mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail, then instead of continuing north toward Lunch Counter, follow Round the Mountain Trail east below Crescent Glacier onto Yakama Nation land, where a separate tribal permit is required and the trail ends at Hellroaring Canyon; the way on, north around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Klickitat and Wilson glacier basins, is a long off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands. Expect a full day just to reach camp in Avalanche Valley, below the Rusk and Wilson glaciers, before a summit attempt.
descent: The descent reverses back down the South Climb to Cold Springs: after topping out via the headwall, parties traverse over toward the summit plateau and descend the standard South Climb route (non-technical snow/scree walk-off, good glissading in early season) back to Lunch Counter and out to the Cold Springs trailhead — a different, easier line than the ascent. This is a walk-off, not a rappel descent. Because the Wilson Glacier Headwall itself is steep snow/ice below cliff bands, a party that needs to bail mid-face rather than finish over the top could reasonably rope down using pickets or V-threads in snow/ice, but this would be an improvised retreat, not a documented standard rappel.
hazards: Steep ice/snow headwall with serac hazard
Persistent rockfall on the surrounding east-side headwalls — among the reasons most Mount Adams headwall routes remain unrepeated
Crevasse navigation on the Wilson Glacier
Rockfall increases sharply as the headwall warms; early-season, cold conditions are essential

waysIn.name: Cold Springs and the Round the Mountain Trail east around the mountain
waysIn.season: Roughly May-Jun for the headwall itself; the surrounding east-side walls are rockfall-prone once warm
waysIn.notes:
From the Cold Springs and South Climb trailhead at about 5,600 ft at the end of the forest road north of Trout Lake, follow South Climb Trail #183 about a mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail.
