Instead of continuing north toward the Lunch Counter, follow the Round the Mountain Trail east and then north, contouring below the Crescent Glacier and around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Klickitat and Wilson glacier basins, crossing the Klickitat Glacier and Big Muddy Creek on the way. This is a long, mostly off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands.

The Wilson descends from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft, and it is split by a rock rib. Expect a full day to reach camp in Avalanche Valley, below the Rusk and Wilson glaciers, before any summit attempt.

This is one of the least-visited and least-documented flanks of the mountain. The descent is not a reversal: parties top out and come down the standard South Climb to Cold Springs.
hazards: Persistent rockfall from the east-side cliff bands, directly over the contouring approach
A steep ice and snow headwall with serac hazard
Crevasse navigation on the Wilson
A long, mostly off-trail traverse with creek crossings and route-finding, and a full day just to reach camp
Rarely climbed, so conditions cannot be inferred from recent traffic and rescue would be slow

name: Eel Glacier / Flypaper Pass
approach: From US-101 at Brinnon, turn onto Dosewallips Road and drive roughly 8.5 miles to the road-end parking — the road beyond has been closed to vehicles since a 2002 flood, with no reopening date on the Olympic National Park road-conditions page updated August 7, 2026; park here (a mountain bike is a real time-saver for the road-walk ahead). Walk about a mile up the closed road and follow the bypass trail around the washout — a short ~0.3-mile detour with a few switchbacks past old-growth trees — then rejoin the abandoned roadbed and continue roughly 5.6 more miles to the Dosewallips Ranger Station (1,600 ft). From the ranger station, pick up the Dosewallips River Trail for 1.4 miles to its junction with the West Fork Dosewallips Trail (Trail #1010); bear onto the West Fork Trail and follow the river upstream past a string of established camps — Dose Forks, Big Timber, Diamond Meadows — to Honeymoon Meadows (3,527 ft, about 8 trail-miles from the ranger station). Expect at least one calf-to-knee-deep ford of the West Fork in this stretch depending on season and snowmelt. Beyond Honeymoon Meadows the trail climbs past Camp Siberia toward Anderson Pass (4,464 ft), the low divide between the Quinault and Dosewallips drainages. Leave the maintained trail here and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to a high camp on a snowy saddle above a small tarn (Anderson/Valkyrie Lake, ~5,100 ft) — most parties budget 7-9 hours trailhead-to-camp. From high camp, traverse above the tarn (often still frozen) and climb the steep snow finger leading up to Flypaper Pass (~6,500 ft); glacier recession has steepened this finger considerably beyond older published descriptions, with the crux section now estimated at 40+ degrees late in the season — plan to be through it before it melts out (ideally spring/early summer) and expect firm or icy snow requiring an ice axe and crampons. Water is reliable along the West Fork the entire way in; at the tarn near high camp it is available only once the tarn melts out, and it is often still frozen, so be ready to melt snow. Carry what you need above that.
descent: Descend the same line used on the ascent — no rappels are required on the standard Eel Glacier/Flypaper Pass route. From the summit, reverse the class 3 scramble and the traverse across the upper Eel Glacier, working back around the rock buttress and re-crossing the bergschrund that cuts across the glacier below Flypaper Pass; the 'schrund forces an end-around to one side or the other, and there is a short (~50 ft) stretch of steep snow just above it that is worth pitching out or plunging pickets for in icy conditions. Climb back up and over Flypaper Pass, then face-in downclimb (or plunge-step/glissade if conditions allow) the steep snow finger back down toward the tarn and high camp — this finger is the real descent crux, reaching an estimated 40+ degrees in its steepest section as the season progresses; a short hand-line or an occasional rappel off a picket or natural anchor is a reasonable precaution late in the year even though it isn't part of the standard beta and most parties downclimb it unroped in good early-season snow. From high camp, retrace the West Fork Dosewallips Trail through Honeymoon Meadows, Diamond Meadows, Big Timber, and Dose Forks back to the Dosewallips Ranger Station, then out the old road and washout bypass to the trailhead. Note that parties climbing Mount Anderson's West Peak by other lines (e.g., a north-face variant) have reported rappelling off natural snow-horn anchors, but that is a different route, not this standard East Peak/Eel Glacier line.
hazards: glacier crevasse fall on the upper Eel Glacier, including large crevasses on its eastern slopes
bergschrund/moat at the head of the Eel Glacier, often hardest to cross in late summer
steep firm/icy snow on the Flypaper Pass finger — glacier recession has steepened it to an estimated 40-45°, well beyond older published descriptions
glide avalanches and cornice-triggered slides off cliffs above the glacier terminus
rockfall and loose, crumbly meta-sedimentary rock on the final Class 3 summit scramble
long, committing wilderness approach (~16+ mi one-way) with no cell coverage
washed-out sections and unbridged fords on the West Fork Dosewallips trail approach

waysIn.name: Dosewallips road walk, West Fork to Anderson Pass and the tarn camp
waysIn.season: Best spring to early summer, while the snow finger below Flypaper Pass is still continuous. By late summer that finger has thinned and steepened and the bergschrund above it has opened
waysIn.notes:
From US-101 at Brinnon, drive Dosewallips Road about 8.5 miles to the road-end parking and leave the car there; the road beyond has been closed to vehicles since the 2002 flood, and the washout itself is about a mile farther on. A mountain bike genuinely saves hours on the road miles. A short bypass trail with a few switchbacks gets round the washout, then the abandoned roadbed resumes for roughly 5.6 miles to the Dosewallips Ranger Station at about 1,600 ft.

From the ranger station take the Dosewallips River Trail 1.4 miles to the West Fork junction, then the West Fork Trail upstream past Dose Forks, Big Timber and Diamond Meadows to Honeymoon Meadows at 3,527 ft, roughly 8 trail miles on. Expect at least one calf-to-knee ford of the West Fork depending on snowmelt, and substantial blowdown — maintenance has lagged since the road closed. Beyond Honeymoon Meadows the trail climbs past Camp Siberia to Anderson Pass at 4,464 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to a camp on the snowy saddle above a small tarn at about 5,100 ft (Anderson or Valkyrie Lake). Most parties take 7-9 hours trailhead to camp. Fill up at the tarn; there is nothing above it.
hazards: Crevasses on the upper Eel Glacier, including large ones on its eastern slopes
Bergschrund at the head of the Eel, hardest to cross late in the season, with a short steep step above it
Flypaper Pass snow finger at 40-45 degrees, firm or icy, steeper than older descriptions
Glide avalanches and cornice-triggered slides off the cliffs above the glacier terminus
Loose, crumbly rock on the final class 3 summit scramble
Unbridged fords and heavy blowdown on the West Fork trail, plus about 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
Long committing approach with no cell coverage

waysIn.name: East Fork Quinault and Enchanted Valley to Anderson Pass from the west
waysIn.season: Same window as the standard side — the pass and the snow finger above it decide the season, not the valley
waysIn.notes:
Anderson Pass is a divide, and the Quinault side of it is a maintained trail too. From the Graves Creek trailhead at the end of the South Shore Quinault road, the East Fork Quinault Trail runs up the valley through Enchanted Valley to the pass. It is a longer valley walk than the Dosewallips side but it is a trail the whole way, with no closed road at the start and no West Fork fords, which in a wet year is the difference between the two.

At Anderson Pass the two approaches become one: leave the maintained trail and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to the tarn camp at about 5,100 ft, then the snow finger to Flypaper Pass.

Mileages published for the Quinault side vary widely with where the count starts and with the current state of the road, so none is quoted here.
hazards: Long valley walk with river crossings and blowdown of its own
40-45 degree firm or icy snow finger at Flypaper Pass
Crevasses on the Eel Glacier and a bergschrund at its head, hardest late season
Glide avalanches and cornice-triggered slides off cliffs above the glacier terminus
Loose, crumbly rock on the final summit scramble
Arriving at Anderson Pass from the west: shelter and climbers' path lie behind you as you crest it
No cell coverage on either side
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the Dosewallips road washout and its long road walk or the West Fork fords at high water are unappealing, or when crossing the Olympics; longer but entirely on maintained trail.

name: Standard Scramble (Switchback / Klahhane Ridge approach)
approach: From the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center parking lot (end of Hurricane Ridge Road, ~17 mi south of Port Angeles via Race St/Hwy 101), start on the paved High Ridge Trail at the east end of the lot. At about 0.3 mi bear toward Sunrise Point/Klahhane Ridge Trail and continue along open, exposed subalpine ridge (alternating meadow and pocket forest) for roughly 2.5 mi to an unsigned junction where a distinct, unmaintained 'climbers trail' splits left (north) off the maintained Klahhane Ridge Trail — this is the start of the true scramble route (sometimes mapped as the Mount Angeles Summit Climbers Trail). A shorter, steeper alternative start exists directly off Hurricane Ridge Road at the Switchback Trail (~mile marker in the last few miles before the visitor center), which gains about 700-800 ft in 0.6 mi to meet the Mount Angeles Trail higher up, cutting off some of the ridge walk. From the climbers-trail junction, the primitive use trail climbs steeply through rocky meadows and thinning forest on the peak's west side — this final push is only about 0.6 mi but does roughly 800 of the route's 2,100 total feet of gain (average grade ~27%, max ~42%), topping out around 6,000 ft at the base of the summit block/gully. Route-finding note from on-the-ground reports: don't scramble the first notch you reach — stay on the faint boot path traversing higher to the actual summit gully. From there, most parties scramble the right/east side of the final block, which is loose, fractured 'rotten' rock (the same line the descent explicitly avoids downclimbing) with only brief but exposed final moves to the true summit (6,454 ft). There is no reliable water past the visitor center (which has a seasonal contact station with restrooms/potable water) — carry all you need. Key hazards: lingering rotten/consolidated snow choking the summit notch/gully well into July and August even in normal years, loose scree and fractured, rockfall-prone rock on the upper scramble, and sustained exposure along the open ridge crest.
descent: Descend the same way you came up as far as the base of the summit block, but do NOT reverse the ascent gully — parties consistently and strongly recommend downclimbing the left (west) side of the summit block/notch instead, since the direct/right-side ascent line is loose, fractured 'rotten' rock that can trigger rockfall or a slide if downclimbed. This is a class 3 scramble downclimb only; there are no fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel stations reported anywhere on the standard route, and roped rappelling is not reported as part of the normal descent — a rope is not standard gear here, though a cautious party could choose to hand-line or belay the notch with a single rope and natural gear (a tree/horn sling) if conditions (verglas, wet rock, inexperienced members) warrant it. Below the block, pick back up the primitive climbers trail, drop back to the Klahhane Ridge Trail junction, and retrace the ridge trail (or the Switchback Trail cutoff, if that was your approach) back to the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center — roughly 3.1 mi and 1.5-2 hours from the summit for the average party. Stay alert on the descent specifically at the loose scree below the block and on the exposed notch downclimb: parties often flag descent, not ascent, as the more dangerous part of this route because of accumulated fatigue plus loose rock underfoot.
hazards: Loose, crumbly rock on the summit block, typical of Olympic sedimentary geology

Exposed Class 3 downclimbing near the top with real fall consequences — parties describe a dirty, loose gully; staying climber's-left on the worn boot path rather than going straight up the scree is important for route-finding and to avoid the worst rockfall funnel
Rockfall from parties climbing above, especially in the narrow crux gully — helmet strongly recommended
Lingering, rotten snow on the approach and in shaded gullies into July in high-snow years
Afternoon thunderstorms and fast-moving weather build over the exposed ridge in late summer; start early and plan to be off the summit block before early afternoon

waysIn.name: Klahhane Ridge climbers' trail from Hurricane Ridge
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Paved path off the east end of the visitor centre lot, then open subalpine ridge for about two and a half miles to an unsigned split. A shorter, steeper start climbs from the Switchback Trail on the road below and joins higher up. Nothing dependable to drink past the visitor centre — carry it all.
hazards: Fractured, rotten rock on the summit block with holds that break
Rockfall funnelling down the crux gully onto anyone below
Rotten snow choking the summit notch into July and August
Exposed Class 3 moves with a fall of well over a hundred feet
Fast-building afternoon storms on a fully exposed ridge
Nothing dependable to drink past the visitor centre

waysIn.name: Switchback Trail up to Klahhane Ridge
waysIn.notes: A steep, short trail from the Hurricane Ridge Road up to the Klahhane Ridge trail, then the same climbers' path to the summit.
hazards: Steep, short trail from the road up to the Klahhane Ridge trail
Fractured, rotten rock on the summit block with holds that break
Rockfall funnelling down the crux gully onto anyone below
Rotten snow in the summit notch into July and August
Exposed Class 3 moves with a long fall
Fast-building afternoon storms on a fully exposed ridge
waysIn.whyThisWay: To save drive time and the ridge walk: it starts from a small lot lower on the road and climbs about 700 feet in 0.6 mile, steeper than the visitor-centre route, joining the same trail.

waysIn.name: Heather Park trail from Heart O' the Hills
waysIn.notes: The long way from low on the Hurricane Ridge Road: the Heather Park trail climbs around the west side of the peak to join the climbers' path.
hazards: Long approach on the Heather Park trail from Heart O' the Hills, around the west side of the peak
Fractured, rotten rock on the summit block with holds that break
Rockfall funnelling down the crux gully onto anyone below
Rotten snow in the summit notch and shaded gullies into July
Exposed Class 3 moves with a long fall
Fast-building afternoon storms on exposed terrain
waysIn.whyThisWay: For a much longer day or a loop, from low on the road and around the west side of the peak; it adds many miles and height compared with the short starts from higher up.

name: Lake Ann Approach Scramble
approach: From the Austin Pass/Artist Point trailhead (paved lot at the end of SR 542, roughly 58 miles / 1.5-2 hr from Bellingham), follow the signed Lake Ann Trail #600, which drops about 800 ft into the Swift Creek headwaters basin before climbing back up to a 4,900-ft saddle northwest of Lake Ann, about 3.9 miles one way; the lake itself is a short way farther down the trail. From the saddle, leave the maintained trail for a boot path heading southwest then south along the ridge crest; where the ridge steepens near 5,300 ft the path contours the east side before the crest re-forms — follow cairns over Peak 5681 and scramble roughly 0.5 mile west along the summit ridge to Mount Ann. Total round trip is about 10.5 miles with roughly 4,000 ft of cumulative elevation gain.
descent: Descent follows the ascent route in reverse: from the summit ridge, scramble east back over Peak 5681 to the point where the boot path drops off the ridge crest, staying high (rather than contouring low) where the path is indistinct to avoid cliffing out above the basin. Regain the 4,900-ft saddle and rejoin the maintained Lake Ann Trail for the descent past the lake and back up over the basin rim to the Austin Pass/Artist Point trailhead. Cairns mark the trickiest sections above ~5,300 ft — losing them in poor visibility is the main routefinding hazard on the way down.
hazards: lingering snowfields on the approach slopes below the 4,900-ft saddle and in the Lake Ann basin, often persisting into August
loose, exposed rock and short scrambling steps along the summit ridge near Peak 5681
fast-changing, exposed weather typical of the Cascade crest between Baker and Shuksan

waysIn.name: Lake Ann Trail #600 to the 4,900 ft saddle, then the boot path and cairns over Peak 5681
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep snow-free; winter and spring ascents are done by experienced parties with mountaineering gear on a stable snowpack
waysIn.notes:
From the Austin Pass / Artist Point trailhead at the end of SR-542, follow the signed Lake Ann Trail #600. It drops about 800 ft into the Swift Creek headwaters basin before climbing back up to a saddle at 4,900 ft northwest of Lake Ann, about 3.9 miles one way; the lake itself is a short way farther down the trail.

From the saddle, leave the maintained trail for a boot path heading southwest then south along the ridge crest. Where the ridge steepens near 5,300 ft the path contours the east side before the crest re-forms; from there follow cairns over Peak 5681 and scramble roughly half a mile west along the summit ridge to Mount Ann.

About 10.5 miles round trip with roughly 4,000 ft of cumulative gain, part of which comes from the fact that the trail loses 800 ft at the start and you pay it back at the end.

Note on the name: this is the Lake Ann below Artist Point on SR-542, not the Lake Ann near Maple Pass. One route has already been recorded with the wrong Lake Ann's trailhead.
hazards: Cairns as the only navigation above 5,300 ft, in both directions
Contouring low on the return, which cliffs out above the Swift Creek basin
An 800 ft descent at the start that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
Two Lake Anns in the North Cascades, and one of them has already been given the wrong trailhead
Lingering snow on the traverse in early season

name: Standard Scramble (Appleton Pass / Boulder Lake approach)
approach: Two approaches reach Appleton Pass, the base for the scramble. The Sol Duc approach is now the practical option: from the Sol Duc Trailhead (about 13 road miles off US-101 via Sol Duc Rd, near Sol Duc Falls), follow the Sol Duc River Trail roughly 4.9 miles upriver, crossing Crystal Creek on a suspension bridge, to the signed Appleton Pass Trail junction, then climb about 2.3 miles and ~2,030 ft through forest and subalpine meadow to Appleton Pass (5,100 ft) — about 7.4 miles and 3,100 ft one-way from the trailhead (trailhead about 1,950 ft to pass 5,100 ft). The alternate Boulder Lake/Elwha approach is now far longer: since Olympic Hot Springs Road washed out and was permanently closed to vehicles beyond Madison Falls, reaching the old Boulder Creek Trailhead adds 8 miles one-way of road walking/biking before another ~7.7 miles of trail (via Boulder Creek Campground and Boulder Lake) to the pass — most parties now use the Sol Duc side. From Appleton Pass, leave the maintained trail and follow a climbers' path north up the ridge crest toward Mount Appleton, working around minor outcrops near the crest, traversing onto the north side across a talus basin near 5,400 ft, then regaining the crest at a rock step near 5,800 ft (marked by a distinct rock horn on its south/left side); pass this on an exposed Class 3 heathery gully/ledge system, then continue up talus and heather to the ~6,000-ft notch below the true summit and on to the top.
descent: Reverse the route, descending the slopes back to Appleton Pass / Boulder Lake.
hazards: Exposed Class 3 scrambling above Appleton Pass: a rock step near 5,800 ft forces an awkward, exposed heathery gully with vegetation ("veggie") holds, and the final approach to the true summit crosses a narrow, exposed "goat ramp."
Loose rock and talus on the upper ridge and basin slopes.
Lingering snow near Appleton Pass and in the basin below the summit into July; NPS recommends an ice axe and self-arrest skills for early-season travel on the approach trail.
Unmarked, braided climbers' path above the pass — easy to wander onto more exposed terrain than intended in fog or low visibility, which is common in the Olympics.
Remote, unpatrolled backcountry setting with unreliable-to-absent cell coverage — a long carry-out for any injury.
Black bear activity in the Boulder Creek/Sol Duc drainages; food and scented items must be stored in an approved bear canister.

waysIn.name: Sol Duc River Trail to Appleton Pass
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Just under five miles upriver, crossing Crystal Creek on a suspension bridge, to the signed pass junction, then a couple of miles and roughly two thousand feet through forest and meadow to the gap. The Boulder Creek side reaches the same pass but is far longer now that the road below it is walked or ridden.
hazards: Exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully where several holds are vegetation
Narrow goat ramp on the final approach to the true summit
Loose rock and talus on the upper ridge and basin slopes
Snow near the pass and in the basin below the summit into July
Braided, unmarked climbers' path that wanders onto steeper ground in fog
Remote backcountry with unreliable cell coverage, long carry-out
Black bear activity in the drainages; scented items need an approved canister

waysIn.name: Boulder Creek from the Elwha
waysIn.notes: From the Elwha side, follow the Boulder Creek trail past the old hot springs and climb to Appleton Pass, where it meets the Sol Duc line. It is the longer way, since the road below the trailhead may have to be walked or biked. Boulder Lake makes a good side camp.
hazards: Longer approach since the road below the Boulder Creek trailhead may have to be walked or biked
Exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully above Appleton Pass with vegetation holds
Narrow goat ramp near the true summit
Loose rock and talus on the upper ridge
Lingering snow near the pass and in the basin into July
Braided climbers' path above the pass that wanders onto steeper ground in fog
Remote with unreliable cell coverage; black bear activity in the drainages
waysIn.whyThisWay: When coming from the Elwha side or making Boulder Lake a camp, though the closed road below the trailhead makes it the longer way in.

name: Southwest Slopes
approach: There is no trail to Mount Arriva itself; the standard approach is a 2-3 day off-trail trip via Fisher Creek Basin and Silent Lakes. From the Easy Pass Trailhead (3,700 ft, SR-20 between mileposts 151 and 152), hike the Easy Pass Trail 3.5-3.6 mi and about 2,800 ft to Easy Pass (~6,500 ft), then descend the west side into Fisher Creek Basin. Near the Fisher Camp junction, a boot path heads east/up-valley but fades after about ten minutes at a pile of avalanche-downed trees; from there travel is cross-country up through meadows to the head of Fisher Creek (~6,000 ft — Fisher Overlook Camp is a good base if short on time). From the head of the valley, climb the roughly 1,000-ft headwall to Silent Lakes (~7,000 ft) via either the obvious snow/ice couloir (steeper than it looks, and melts into a loose rock gully by late season) or the broken heather/cliff ramps to its left; ice axe and crampons are useful here into mid-summer. From a camp at Upper Silent Lake, a roughly 1-mile westerly traverse across heather leads to a 7,200-ft saddle, then a rising traverse across a talus bowl gains a key 7,800-ft notch on Arriva's south ridge for the final scramble to the summit.
descent: Reverse the route.
hazards: extensive loose ('chossy') rock on the summit ridge's gullies and ledges — rockfall onto climbers below is a documented hazard
steep snow/ice in the Silent Lakes approach couloir, the technical crux of the trip (not the summit scrambling); it degrades into a loose rock gully by late season
long off-trail routefinding through Fisher Creek Basin with no maintained tread beyond the Fisher Camp junction
avalanche paths on the flanks of Ragged Ridge near Easy Pass in early season
black bears frequent Fisher Creek Basin and the Easy Pass meadows
afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer on this exposed ridge

waysIn.name: Easy Pass, Fisher Creek Basin and Silent Lakes
waysIn.season: Late July through September for the most reliable snow-free travel. An axe and often crampons are still worth carrying into July for the headwall couloir and the north side of Easy Pass. The highway itself is shut in winter.
waysIn.notes: There is no trail to this peak. From the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20 the maintained trail climbs to Easy Pass, and from there you descend the west side into Fisher Creek Basin. Near the Fisher Camp junction a boot path heads up-valley but fades within about ten minutes at a pile of avalanche-downed trees; from there travel is cross-country up through meadows to the head of Fisher Creek, where an overlook camp works well as a base if you are short of time. From the head of the valley the headwall to Silent Lakes goes either by the obvious snow and ice couloir — steeper than it looks from below, and degrading into a loose rock gully by late season — or by the broken heather and cliff ramps to its left. An axe, and often crampons, are useful here into midsummer. From a camp at Upper Silent Lake, a roughly westerly traverse across heather leads to a saddle around 7,200 ft, then a rising traverse across a talus bowl gains the notch on the peak's south ridge where the scrambling starts.
hazards: extensive loose rock in the summit ridge's gullies and ledges, with rockfall onto anyone below
steep snow and ice in the headwall couloir to Silent Lakes — the real technical crux of the trip, not the summit scrambling
long off-trail route-finding through Fisher Creek Basin with no tread beyond the Fisher Camp junction
avalanche paths on the flanks near Easy Pass in early season
black bears through Fisher Creek Basin and the Easy Pass meadows
afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed ridge

name: Cockscomb Ridge
approach: From the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (~3,700 ft) at the end of Glacier Creek Road (FR 39), follow Trail 677 through old growth to the fork at about two miles and take the right-hand climbers' path up the Hogsback moraine to camp near 6,000 ft at the edge of the Coleman Glacier. From camp, rope up and cross the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier heading northeast — roughly 2-3 hours of crevassed travel — and take low-to-moderate snow ramps to the foot of the ridge at about 7,500-7,800 ft. Thin snow bridges over a crevasse maze are the main hazard on this crossing.
descent: Descend Coleman-Deming or Easton
hazards: Loose, exposed rock on the ridge crest, worst later in the season
Crevasses and bergschrunds crossing the Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers on approach
Rockfall potential (PG13) below the Cockscomb Tower
Late-season parties may need to detour onto the Park Glacier and climb its AI3 headwall to bypass the Tower

waysIn.name: Heliotrope Ridge, the Hogsback and the Coleman-Roosevelt crossing
waysIn.season: spring to early summer
waysIn.notes:
Glacier Creek Road (FR 39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, then Trail 677 through old growth to the fork at about two miles. Take the right-hand climbers' path up the crest of the Hogsback moraine to the camps near 6,000 ft beside the Coleman Glacier, the same camp used for the Coleman-Deming and the North Ridge.

From camp the route ropes up and heads northeast, crossing the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier. Expect two to three hours of glacier travel through a crevasse field before low-to-moderate snow ramps lead to the foot of the ridge.
hazards: Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers
Bergschrunds below and on the ridge
Loose rock on the ridge, worse as the snow melts out
Icefall on the ramps that skirt the towers
Rockfall potential below the Cockscomb Tower
Late-season detour onto the Park Glacier and its AI3 headwall may be needed to bypass the Tower

waysIn.name: Artist Point and Ptarmigan Ridge to the Park Glacier
waysIn.notes: From Artist Point at the end of the Mount Baker Highway, take the Chain Lakes trail to the Ptarmigan Ridge junction and follow Ptarmigan Ridge west to Camp Kiser where the trail ends. Cross the Rainbow Glacier onto the Park Glacier and camp near the Portals, the usual base for the Cockscomb from this side. It is a much longer approach than Heliotrope Ridge.
hazards: Rainbow and Park Glacier crossings, crevassed, from Camp Kiser
Much longer approach: Chain Lakes trail, Ptarmigan Ridge to Camp Kiser, then onto the glacier
Bergschrunds below and on the ridge
Loose rock on the ridge, worse as the snow melts out
Icefall on the ramps that skirt the towers
Rockfall potential below the Cockscomb Tower; late-season Park Glacier AI3 headwall bypass of the Tower
waysIn.whyThisWay: When coming at the ridge from the Artist Point side, for example linking it with other Park Glacier objectives; far longer than Heliotrope, and the road there is closed by snow much of the year.

name: Coleman–Deming Glacier
approach: Coleman-Deming on Mount Baker starts at Heliotrope Ridge TH (about 3,700 ft) via Glacier Creek Road (FS 39). Gain about 2,300 ft over roughly 3 miles through forest and alpine meadows, crossing Grouse, Kulshan, and Heliotrope Creeks to reach Hogsback Camp (6,000 ft). Cross creeks in early morning before afternoon glacial melt surge. From Hogsback, rope up on Coleman and Deming Glaciers (crevasses, route-finding). Roman Wall (~40°) is the crux—steep snow between Deming Glacier and summit plateau. Most parties summit on day two.
descent: This is a walk-off, not a rappel descent - reverse the ascent line. From the summit plateau, descend the Roman Wall carefully (many parties down-climb facing in on the steepest section, especially if icy or in a whiteout), back onto the Deming Glacier, across the Baker-Colfax saddle, and back down the Coleman Glacier icefall to the Hogsback and high camp. Route-finding through the Coleman icefall's crevasse maze is often trickier on descent (softer afternoon snow, sun-cupped and collapsing snow bridges); parties note snowbridges on this stretch have collapsed in late season and required an end-run around crevasses on climbers' left. No technical rappels are used on the standard route in normal conditions - this is graded a basic glacier mountaineering line. From Hogsback, retrace the Heliotrope Ridge Trail back to the trailhead.
hazards: Crevasse falls on the Coleman and Deming glaciers, worse late season
The Roman Wall — final steep snow slope to ~40°
Rockfall in the Black Buttes saddle area
Soft afternoon snow and hidden crevasses on descent
Heliotrope Creek crossing on the approach trail — fast water and slick rocks, most serious early season
Bergschrund crossing where the route gains the upper Coleman/Deming glaciers or the Roman Wall saddle; can require a snow-bridge or step-across, worse late season.

A serac on Colfax Peak, directly above the route, periodically fractures and calves large icefall onto the Coleman-Deming Glacier below -- a known, recurring objective hazard on this route, not a one-off event

waysIn.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trail #677 to the Hogsback
waysIn.season: May-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Glacier Creek Road (FS 39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead. Trail 677 switchbacks up through old growth and avalanche chutes, crossing Grouse, Kulshan and Heliotrope Creeks. Those crossings are fed by glacier melt and run highest in the afternoon, so cross early on the way in and expect them to be worse coming out.

At roughly two and a quarter miles the trail forks: left continues to the Coleman Glacier overlook, right is the climbers' path onto the moraine crest known as the Hogsback. Standard camp sits at about 6,000 ft, around three miles and 2,300 ft above the car. Meltwater usually runs at the Hogsback camp itself; above the camp there is nothing but what you melt. Some parties camp higher, toward the Black Buttes at around 7,200 ft.

Glacier Creek Road has a history of washing out; when it has been closed low, parties have added several miles of road on foot or bike before reaching the sign-in kiosk.
hazards: creek crossings surge with afternoon glacial melt
annual avalanche debris off the Colfax Peak ridge across the standard track
crevasses on the Coleman and upper Deming
whiteout navigation on the featureless upper glacier and summit plateau
no water above the Hogsback camp

name: Coleman Headwall
approach: Start from the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (~3,700 ft, reached via Glacier Creek Rd 39, which reopened to vehicles all the way to the trailhead in August 2026 after flood repairs; it has washed out before, so check its status with the Mount Baker Ranger District before you go). Trail 677 climbs through old-growth forest and flower-filled avalanche chutes; watch for a couple of unbridged creek crossings that can be awkward early season or after rain. At roughly 2.25 mi the maintained trail forks — the left fork continues to the Coleman Glacier overlook, the right fork is the climbers' path that drops toward the moraine and begins the real work. Past Kulshan Cabin's former site (~4,800–5,000 ft, last reliable running water before camp), the trail climbs steeply up the crest of the lateral moraine known as the Hogsback. Most parties establish high camp somewhere on or near the Hogsback between about 6,500 and 7,200 ft — either on the ridge itself or on the flat benches toward the Black Buttes/Roman Nose — roughly 3–3.5 mi and ~3,000 ft above the trailhead. Above camp there is no water except what you melt. From camp, rope up for glacier travel and cross the broken lower Coleman Glacier: the line generally trends up toward ~8,000 ft to meet the North Ridge tracks before dropping back down and cutting under the Roman Nose to reach the base of the headwall near 8,500 ft. This glacier crossing is a genuine route-finding crux that changes year to year — it can involve weaving around large crevasses, crossing questionable snow bridges, and occasionally a committing, barely-reversible crevasse jump or a short vertical step to get established at the base. Because the headwall and the Black Buttes shed rock and ice as the day warms, most parties leave camp in the pre-dawn hours (11 p.m.–4:30 a.m. starts are typical) specifically to be on or past the exposed glacier crossing and lower headwall before the sun hits it.
descent: Descent is via the standard Coleman-Deming route, not back down the headwall, and it is a non-technical walk/downclimb with no rappelling required. From the summit plateau, drop down the Roman Wall — a ~35-45° snow slope that most parties downclimb or glissade in a boot-ski — to the saddle between the Black Buttes and Baker's summit dome. From there continue down onto the lower Coleman Glacier, roping back up for crevasse hazard, and retrace the ascent line (or a lower, more direct crossing) back to high camp. From camp, walk back out the Hogsback moraine crest and Heliotrope Ridge Trail 677 to the trailhead — allow 3-4 hours from summit to camp and another 1.5-2.5 hours from camp to the car, longer if the road washout adds its extra miles. No trip reports for this route describe fixed rappels on the standard descent; parties instead glissade/downclimb the Roman Wall on foot. The one place technical rope work sometimes appears is on-route, not on descent proper: if the final bergschrund below the summit ice cap can't be climbed or downclimbed cleanly, some parties build a quick picket or ice-screw/v-thread anchor to belay or lower across it — this is a crux-mitigation tactic during the ascent, not part of the standard walk-off. Because the Roman Wall and glacier crossing are on the sunny south/east aspect, get over them before the snow goes soft; the same crevasse and icefall hazards from the approach apply in reverse on the way down.
hazards: Steep ice/snow headwall with serac hazard above
Bergschrund at the base of the headwall
Crevasse navigation on the Coleman Glacier
Icefall and rockfall risk rises sharply once the sun hits the face — nearly all parties climb the headwall before or around sunrise

waysIn.name: Heliotrope Ridge to a high Hogsback camp
waysIn.season: late Apr-Jun
waysIn.notes:
Heliotrope Ridge trailhead via Glacier Creek Road. Trail 677 through old growth and avalanche chutes with a couple of unbridged creek crossings, then at about two and a quarter miles take the right-hand climbers' fork off the maintained trail onto the moraine. Past the old Kulshan Cabin site — the last running water — climb the Hogsback crest.

Parties on this route camp higher than the standard Coleman-Deming crowd, commonly around 6,700 ft and sometimes as high as 7,200, either on the ridge itself or on the flats toward the Black Buttes and the Roman Nose. Above camp everything is melted snow.

From camp the line goes up the centre of the broken Coleman. This is the real crux of the day: weaving round large crevasses, crossing bridges of uncertain quality, and occasionally a committing jump or a short vertical step to get established. It changes materially from season to season.

Starts are early — anything from late evening to half past four in the morning — specifically to be through the exposed glacier and onto the lower headwall before the sun loosens the wall and the Black Buttes above.

Glacier Creek Road has washed out more than once, most recently in the December 2025 floods, and it reopened to the trailhead in August 2026. When it is closed low it adds several miles on foot or bike before the kiosk, so check its status before a trip.
hazards: the Coleman Glacier crossing itself — large crevasses, questionable bridges, occasionally a barely reversible move
rockfall and icefall off the headwall and the Black Buttes once the sun is on them
bergschrund at the base of the wall every season
no water above camp

name: Coleman Ski Descent
approach: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (about 3,700 ft) at the end of Glacier Creek Road (FR 39) and follow Trail 677 through old growth, crossing several creeks that run higher in the afternoon than the morning. At about two miles and 4,700 ft you pass the former Kulshan Cabin site, then a signed junction: the left fork goes to the Coleman Glacier overlook and the right fork is the climbers' trail. Take the climbers' trail steeply up the Hogsback moraine ridge to the edge of the Coleman Glacier near 6,000 ft, where most parties camp. In winter and spring the road may be gated miles short of the trailhead, which adds distance, and the glacier is skinned from there toward the Deming.
descent: Ski or walk off by the way you came up. From the summit plateau drop down the Roman Wall, a snow slope of 35 to 45 degrees that is usually downclimbed or skied with care when it is icy, onto the Deming Glacier. Cross the saddle and ski the Coleman Glacier's upper slopes, picking a line through its crevasses and icefall; snow bridges sag in afternoon sun, and late season can force an end-run to climbers' left. Aim for the Hogsback and the climbers' trail junction near 4,700 ft, then follow Trail 677 out. Cloud can close in fast, so follow your up-track.

name: Easton Glacier
approach: From the Park Butte/Schriebers Meadow Trailhead (~3,360 ft, end of FR 13/Sulphur Creek Road), the route follows Park Butte Trail 603. Cross Sulphur Creek on a footbridge/log crossing near the start (can be a ford in high water), then climb through Schriebers Meadow and forest switchbacks to Morovitz Meadows (about 2.25 miles in). For the Easton Glacier route, leave the Park Butte trail here and bear right onto Railroad Grade Trail 603.2, which climbs the crest of a lateral moraine (the 'railroad grade') with the Easton Glacier dropping away on the right. High camp options are at established sites around 5,600 ft (roughly 3.75 miles from the trailhead) or at Sandy Camp, a cluster of rock-walled tent pads at the moraine's end near 5,900-6,000 ft where the maintained trail effectively ends and glacier travel begins. From Sandy Camp, gain the toe of the Easton Glacier, rope up, and ascend the broad glacier, generally staying climbers' right (east) of the major crevasse bands, to the base of the Roman Wall. Hazards: exposed moraine crest can be loose/exposed in wind, Sulphur Creek crossing can be difficult during peak snowmelt, and there is no reliable water source above Morovitz Meadows other than melting snow.
descent: Non-technical walk-off: reverse the ascent line. From the summit plateau, descend the Roman Wall - a sustained 35-45 degree snow/ice slope that is the crux of the whole route and can be quite icy and rockfall-prone late season; many parties face in and plunge-step or down-climb it carefully - then back down the Easton Glacier to Sandy Camp/high camp, generally retracing the up-track and staying right of the major crevasses. From camp, follow Railroad Grade back down to Morovitz Meadows and out Park Butte Trail 603 to the trailhead. No rappels are used on the standard route; this is one of the two easiest ways up Mount Baker and is regularly guided as a walk-up glacier climb.
hazards: Crevasse navigation on the Easton Glacier, especially late season
The Roman Wall finish to ~40°
Soft afternoon snow on the long south-facing descent
Whiteout navigation on the broad open glacier
Snowmobile traffic in the Mt. Baker National Recreation Area on the lower approach into early summer
Rocky Creek crossing near Schriebers Meadow can be difficult in high runoff or when the seasonal bridge is out — a post-holing/ford hazard
Bergschrund crossing above the toe of the Easton Glacier, typically snow-bridged early/mid season but can require a detour or step-across late season.

waysIn.name: Park Butte Trail 603 and the Railroad Grade to Sandy Camp
waysIn.season: May-Sep
waysIn.notes:
Schriebers Meadow / Park Butte trailhead at about 3,400 ft, at the end of the Sulphur Creek road. Cross Sulphur Creek near the start — bridged or on logs, but a genuine ford during peak snowmelt — then climb through the meadow and forest switchbacks.

At about two and a quarter miles a signed junction sends you right onto the Railroad Grade Trail 603.2. Stone steps take you up onto the crest of the lateral moraine. There are three established camp areas along the way; Sandy Camp at about 5,900 ft is the usual one for climbing, roughly four miles in with 2,600 ft of gain.

Above Morovitz Meadows there is no reliable water other than melted snow.
hazards: Sulphur Creek crossing during peak melt
exposed, loose moraine crest in wind
crevasses on the broad Easton, worse late season
volcanic gas and unstable ground at Sherman Crater
no water above Morovitz Meadows

name: Park Glacier Headwall
approach: From the northeast via Chain Lakes Trail to Ptarmigan Ridge. From Artist Point parking, take Chain Lakes Trail (682) to Ptarmigan Ridge Trail (682.1) junction. Continue about 3 miles west along the ridge to Coleman Pinnacle base, then 0.5 miles to Camp Kiser (~6,000 ft).
descent: Reverse the ascent: descend the Park Glacier, recross the Rainbow Glacier to camp near the Portals, then walk back along Ptarmigan Ridge to Artist Point, taking the lower line north of Coleman Pinnacle to avoid regaining height. Going down the Coleman-Deming instead ends at Heliotrope Ridge on the far side of the mountain and needs a car shuttle.
hazards: Steep ice headwall with serac hazard
Crevasse navigation on the Park Glacier
Remote NE-side approach

waysIn.name: Artist Point, Ptarmigan Ridge and the Portals
waysIn.season: Jun-Aug
waysIn.notes: Drive the Mount Baker Highway to its end at Artist Point. Start on Chain Lakes Trail 682 for about a mile to the Ptarmigan Ridge junction, then follow Ptarmigan Ridge Trail 682.1 along the crest. Three miles from that junction the trail reaches the base of Coleman Pinnacle, and half a mile further is Camp Kiser — about four and a half miles in from Artist Point. The snow on this stretch does not melt out until late in the season, so early parties face a long slog and steep snow chutes, while later parties get easier walking and much harder route-finding as the bootpaths multiply and diverge. Beyond Camp Kiser the graded tread ends and a bootpath threads the rocky ground of the Portals. From there the route drops onto the Rainbow Glacier, crosses onto the Park Glacier, and heads up toward the headwall with the Cockscomb above it. Most parties camp near the Portals. Camp Kiser itself is a nondescript flat near 6,000 ft, not a high camp on the mountain proper.
hazards: long steep snow chutes on the approach early in the season
multiplying bootpaths through the Portals once the snow melts
crevasses on the Rainbow and Park Glaciers
Camp Kiser is unmarked and easily walked through

name: Squak Glacier
approach: From the Park Butte/Schriebers Meadow trailhead area, take the Scott Paul Trail; around 4,600 ft leave the maintained trail for the climbers' path to Crag View camp (~6,500 ft, about 3.5 mi from the trailhead with roughly 3,300 ft of gain).
descent: From the summit, descend the upper mountain via the Easton route, then rejoin the Squak Glacier's descent line back past Sherman Peak to Crag View camp and the trailhead.
hazards: Late-season bergschrund formation is the route's main technical obstacle.
Nearby Sherman Crater has minor ongoing fumarole/steam activity.

waysIn.name: Scott Paul Trail to Crag View
waysIn.season: best early season, May-Jul
waysIn.notes:
Same parking as the Easton route, at Schriebers Meadow. The Scott Paul Trail branches off within about a hundred feet of the trailhead and contours around the base of the mountain through forest, meadow and moraine.

After a few miles an unmarked junction sends the route north onto a steep climbers' path. That path leads to Crag View camp at about 6,500 ft, roughly three and a half miles in with 3,300 ft of gain. The Squak Glacier is gained near Point 6513, which some maps label Crag View.

This is the early-season choice on Baker's south side; later in the year a bergschrund develops on the route that is awkward to get past. Higher up the route merges with the Easton line near Sherman Crater.
hazards: unmarked trail junction at about 4,600 ft, easily walked past
exposed class 3 finish on the ridge to Crag View
bergschrund on the Squak that becomes difficult later in the season
volcanic gas near Sherman Crater where the route joins the Easton

name: South Slopes
approach: Standard approach: drive Highway 20 to the Canyon Creek Trailhead near milepost 141, west of Rainy Pass and follow the Mill Creek/Azurite Pass Trail (#755) up Canyon Creek then Mill Creek — about 11 miles (roughly 6 along Canyon Creek, then 5 up Mill Creek) to the site of the defunct Azurite Mine, then a further ~3 increasingly faint, brush-choked miles (slide alder and downed timber are common since the trail has seen little maintenance since the mine closed) to roughly the 14-mile mark, where a boot path continues about 1.5 more miles to Azurite Pass (6,680+ ft). A longer alternate, more often used for combined Azurite-Ballard trips, starts at the West Fork Methow River Trailhead (#480) near River Bend Campground: follow that trail ~8 miles to the PCT, then the PCT south ~1.5 miles to Horse Heaven Camp before joining the Mill Creek Trail to the pass — this option runs closer to 25 miles round trip with about 6,000 ft of elevation gain.
descent: Descend the south slopes, retracing the ascent into the basin.
hazards: long, unmaintained Mill Creek Trail approach choked with slide alder and downed timber
routefinding on broad, featureless upper slopes and gullies
loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge crux
lingering snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
afternoon thunderstorms and lightning exposure on the open upper mountain
very remote location — a long, difficult evacuation if injured

waysIn.name: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
waysIn.season: Late July to September
waysIn.notes: This is the approach the peak is normally catalogued under and the one that pairs naturally with Azurite. It runs from Highway 20 up Canyon Creek and then Mill Creek on tread that has seen little maintenance since the mine closed, where slide alder and downed timber are the recurring complaint and parties routinely lose the path entirely for stretches. Camp is usually made near the old mine or in the basin above it. Note that the point long marked on maps as Mount Ballard is a lower north sub-summit; the true high point lies about 1,100 ft further south and is slightly higher.
hazards: Slide alder and downed timber on an unmaintained approach trail; the path is often lost
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Open upper mountain with full lightning exposure
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured

waysIn.name: South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge
waysIn.season: July to September
waysIn.notes: The other side of the mountain, approached from the Slate Creek road system rather than from Mill Creek, and the line most parties who climb this peak actually use. It is shorter, the forest below camp is comparatively brush-free, and the route-finding above camp is far more legible than on the Mill Creek side, at the cost of one genuinely steep step low down and some exposed ledge work near the top. Snow conditions change this route's character completely: a filled-in slot low down and firm snow in the upper cirque make for fast travel, while dry late-season conditions leave loose rock and slippery vegetation. Camp is normally made in a scree basin below the east ridge.
hazards: Steep vegetated step through the lowest cliff band, the hardest ground on the route
Exposed ledge traverse above the high saddle
Loose rock in the summit gully with a party stacked below
Steep snow in the east cirque into midsummer
Full lightning exposure on the open upper mountain
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
waysIn.whyThisWay: When a shorter, less brushy approach with clearer route-finding is wanted and the Slate Creek road is passable; snow in the upper cirque speeds travel.

waysIn.name: West Fork Methow and the PCT
waysIn.notes: From the West Fork Methow trailhead, up to the Pacific Crest Trail by way of Horse Heaven Camp and over to the Mill Creek side. Longer, and usually chosen for combined trips despite the extra mileage.
hazards: Long approach up the West Fork Methow to the Pacific Crest Trail and over to the Mill Creek side
Slide alder and downed timber on the unmaintained Mill Creek approach
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Full lightning exposure; very remote with a long, difficult evacuation
waysIn.whyThisWay: On a combined trip with neighbouring peaks, since the trail and Pacific Crest Trail avoid the overgrown Mill Creek tread at the cost of extra mileage.

name: Elwha Basin Scramble
approach: No maintained trail leads directly to Mount Barnes — it is a cross-country side-trip off the Bailey Range Traverse. Two main approaches: (1) West via Sol Duc Trailhead — Sol Duc River Trail up to Bogachiel Peak/High Divide (filling water at Heart Lake, the last reliable source for miles), then off-trail east along the Bailey Range crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin, and Stephen Peak to Bear Pass — roughly 3-5 days of travel before reaching Barnes. (2) East via the Elwha River Trail — historically from Whiskey Bend Trailhead (about 26 mi one way with ~6,100 ft gain to the trail's end near Elwha Basin/Dodwell-Rixon Pass); since a washout closed Olympic Hot Springs Road to vehicles at Madison Falls, Whiskey Bend has had no car access, adding an extra 6.2 mi one-way walk or bike from the Madison Falls parking area just to reach the trailhead. From a camp near Bear Pass or a nearby meadow, the final summit push contours scree and lingering snow patches southeast, then curls north on a boot track up a moderate scree slope to the Class 2 summit — a few hours round trip once camp is established.
descent: Reverse the scramble and the long trail back out.
hazards: deep interior isolation near the Elwha Basin
committing multi-day access
'the maze' — dense slide-alder bushwhacking between the Elwha River and Elwha Basin that can take hours even on a known route
the Elwha Snowfinger has largely melted out and is no longer a dependable ascent/descent ramp — expect steep scree, crumbly slabs, and an icy snow-hump crossing instead
loose, fragmented ('chossy') Eocene sedimentary rock with few solid cracks for protection
no maintained trail, cell coverage, or reliable water for long stretches of the cross-country route
high self-rescue burden — NPS reported 9 helicopter rescues among roughly 150 permitted Bailey Range parties in 2018

waysIn.name: Bailey Range crest to Bear Pass
waysIn.season: Late July to mid-September
waysIn.notes: This peak has two genuinely different journeys to it: the western one from the Sol Duc over the High Divide and along the Bailey crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin and Stephen Peak, and the eastern one up the Elwha with a long road walk or ride added at the start. Both take days. Almost every ascent is a side-summit off a traverse rather than a trip in its own right.
hazards: Days of off-trail travel along the Bailey crest with no quick bail-out and no cell coverage
Firm snow on the small glacier below Bear Pass: axe and traction needed
Few reliable water sources beyond Heart Lake on the long crest traverse
Loose, fragmented sedimentary rock with few solid cracks for protection
Steep scree and lingering snow patches on the contour to the summit scree slope
Deep interior isolation; a high self-rescue burden with helicopter evacuations recorded

waysIn.name: Up the Elwha to Elwha Basin
waysIn.notes: The eastern way: follow the Elwha River trail up the full length of the valley past Hayes River and Chicago Camp to Elwha Basin, then climb onto the peak from the basin. It takes several days, and a road walk or bike ride may be needed to reach the trailhead.
hazards: 'The maze': dense slide-alder bushwhacking between the Elwha River and Elwha Basin that can take hours
The Elwha Snowfinger has largely melted out; expect steep scree, crumbly slabs and an icy snow hump instead of a ramp
Hazardous fords on the upper Elwha in high water
Closed road adds a 6-7 mile walk or bike ride each way before the trail even starts
Loose, fragmented sedimentary rock with few solid cracks for protection
Committing multi-day access in deep interior with a high self-rescue burden
waysIn.whyThisWay: When approaching from the Elwha side rather than traversing the Bailey crest from the Sol Duc, accepting a several-day walk and possibly a long road walk at the start.

name: Southwest Route
approach: From Trinity Trailhead (end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200, about 23 miles up-road from WA-207 near Lake Wenatchee), three approaches reach Mount Berge's flanks within the Glacier Peak Wilderness. (1) Southwest approach: via the Little Giant Trail #1518, whose own trailhead sits at 2,600 ft about mile 19 of Chiwawa River Road; the trail climbs to Little Giant Pass (~10 mi round trip to the pass alone), drops into the Napeequa River valley, then follows a climbers' path upstream to the end of maintained tread at the creek draining Berge's southwest side. A steep, intermittent boot track then climbs through timber to treeline and opens into the peak's southwest basin used for this scramble route. (2) East/Buck Creek approach: from Trinity, follow the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 about 2 miles to its junction with Buck Creek Trail #1513, then continue on Buck Creek Trail roughly 4-5 miles into the basin shared with Mount Cleator and Buck Mountain on Berge's east side. (3) North/High Pass approach: continue past the Buck Creek junction to Buck Creek Pass, then take the climbers' path over High Pass, contouring south under Berge's north side near Point 7839 — longest by mileage but with the least off-trail travel. All three options involve 15+ miles of hiking round trip and are typically done as multi-day trips.
descent: Reverse the southwest slopes back into the approach basins.
hazards: loose scree
rockfall
remote terrain
unbridged or damaged creek crossings on the Napeequa River and Buck Creek approaches
avalanche and steep snow terrain in early season (June-early July)
brush and blowdown on unmaintained climbers' paths above trail's end

waysIn.name: Little Giant Trail #1518 over the pass and down into the Napeequa
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable. The Chiwawa ford at the very start of this trail is waist-deep and swift in early season and is only reliably safe in late-summer and autumn low water
waysIn.notes:
The Little Giant Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft roughly mile 19 of Chiwawa River Road, three miles down-valley of Trinity. The trail begins with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River, right at the start — there is no way around it and it is the gate on the whole approach.

Trail #1518 then climbs steeply and badly-eroded to Little Giant Pass at 6,463 ft, with a small spring a few hundred feet below the pass at about 6,250 ft that is the last dependable water before the high basins. Maintained tread effectively ends at the pass.

From the pass the route drops toward the Louis Creek and Napeequa basin, then follows a climbers' path upstream to the end of tread at the creek draining Berge's south-west side. A steep, intermittent boot track climbs through timber to treeline and opens into the south-west basin. A narrow notch at about 7,840 ft in the ridge crest links the Louis Creek basin to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face, and gaining it is exposed scrambling.

All options to this peak are 15-plus miles round trip and are multi-day trips.
hazards: Unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River at the very start of Little Giant Trail, waist-deep and swift outside late-season low water
Steep, badly eroded trail to Little Giant Pass and no maintained tread beyond it
Exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft where a slip has serious consequences
Loose scree and rockfall in the south-west basin and gully
North and west faces are cliffy; going straight up from High Pass does not work
Short fourth-class step to the true north summit
Steep snow and moat on the snow finger in early season (June-early July)

waysIn.name: Trinity and Buck Creek, or the High Pass high route from Buck Creek Pass
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable
waysIn.notes:
Two other ways reach the same mountain from the Trinity side.

The east approach: from Trinity, follow Chiwawa River Trail #1550 about two miles to the Buck Creek Trail #1513 junction, then Buck Creek Trail roughly four to five miles into the basin Berge shares with Mount Cleator and Buck Mountain on its east side.

The north approach: continue past the Buck Creek junction to Buck Creek Pass, then take the climbers' path over High Pass and contour south under Berge's north side near Point 7839. This is the longest by mileage and has the least off-trail travel, which is the trade it offers.

Both involve unbridged or damaged creek crossings and both are multi-day. FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which affects the drive to Trinity.
hazards: Berge's north face is cliffy and the direct line from High Pass does not go; this approach passes beneath it
Unbridged or damaged creek crossings on the Buck Creek approach
Brush and blowdown on unmaintained climbers' paths above the end of tread
Exposed scrambling to gain the narrow 7,840 ft notch in the ridge crest
Loose scree and rockfall in the south-west basin and gully
Exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft on the final climb
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, lengthening the drive-in to Trinity
Remote country, 15+ miles round trip, usually multi-day
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the unbridged Chiwawa ford at Little Giant is too high to cross; the High Pass line is longer but has the least off-trail travel.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Drive to the Crater Creek Trailhead (4,750 ft): from Twisp, take WA-20 east 2 miles to WA-153, then south 12 miles to County Rd 1029/1034 (signed for Foggy Dew Campground) and follow it about 6 miles as it becomes FR 4340 - pavement ends around mile 4 (bear right) - then continue on FR 4340-300 roughly 4.6 more miles to the trailhead parking area (vault toilet, stock ramp, no potable water). From the trailhead, hike the Eagle Lakes Trail #431 about 5-6 miles, gaining roughly 2,400 ft, to the basin holding Lower Eagle Lake (6,490 ft) and Upper Eagle Lake (7,110 ft) - the trail passes an overlook of Lower Eagle Lake around mile 5.5 with a junction just beyond it (left to Lower Eagle Lake/Horsehead Pass, right ~0.5 mi to Upper Eagle Lake). For the direct line, leave the trail near Upper Eagle Lake and head northwest through larch stands toward a notch, staying right of the prominent rock wall above the lake; scramble slabby rock to get above a lower cliff band, then traverse left below the next cliff band and climb steep, loose scree/rock to just below the summit block for the Class 3 finish.
descent: Reverse the route. The south and southeast gullies and slopes below the summit are loose gravel and slab: in mid June a slab layer slid free near 7,400 ft, and in August the gully south of the top was slow going. Descend one at a time and do not stand below a partner.
hazards: loose talus and scree, worst on the steep section just below the summit block
long approach (roughly 5-6 miles and ~2,400 ft to Upper Eagle Lake before the climb even starts)
exposed Class 3 finish through slabby rock and cliff bands - easy to get cliffed out if you stray off the standard line
lingering snow in the cirque and summit gullies into July
swarming mosquitoes at Eagle Lakes in July, especially at unshielded lakeshore camps
remote wilderness terrain with no reliable cell coverage

waysIn.name: Eagle Lakes Trail #431 to Upper Eagle Lake
waysIn.season: Roughly July through October, once road and trail are snow-free. Snow lingers in the notch through the lower cliff band into summer and makes the route-finding harder.
waysIn.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the forest-road spur, fill out the self-issue wilderness permit and start up Eagle Lakes Trail #431. The tread crosses Crater Creek on a bridge early on — stay straight where the Crater Creek Trail splits — and climbs steadily, with an established camp roughly halfway. Past an overlook of the lower lake the trail reaches a junction: the left branch goes to the lower lake and the pass beyond, the right-hand spur climbs a half mile to Upper Eagle Lake. Take the spur. The upper lake sits in a cirque with established campsites and is the last reliable water and the staging point before the off-trail push, which starts from its northwest shore.
hazards: Route-finding through the cliff bands is genuinely tricky, especially with snow still lying in the notch
Steep, loose scree and rock between the bands, with a loose path worn straight up it
Pushing too far climber's right onto the better rock cliffs you out at the end of the ridge
An eight-foot chimney below the summit block with poor handholds in small pebbles and sand — a slip there would be serious
The summit rises over 1,300 ft above the upper lake in about a third of a mile
No water above the lake

waysIn.name: Horsehead Pass and the west slopes
waysIn.season: July through October. The west side melts out and stays passable later in the autumn than the shaded notch on the east side.
waysIn.notes: The easier alternative stays on the main trail past the Upper Eagle Lake spur, continues to the lower lake and climbs to Horsehead Pass, then gains the peak's west slopes from the far side of the crest. It trades the exposed scrambling for distance and a long, loose walk-up, and is the sensible choice for a party that does not want the cliff-band route-finding or that finds snow still lying in the notch above the upper lake.
hazards: Long and described as annoyingly loose underfoot for its whole length
No water once you leave the lake basin
Exposed crest with no shelter from afternoon weather
waysIn.whyThisWay: When snow still fills the notch above the upper lake or the cliff-band route-finding is unwanted; a longer, looser walk-up from the west.

name: Tribute to Richard
approach: Drive to the Crater Creek Trailhead (4,750 ft, 48.2205 / -120.26801). From Twisp take SR 20 south 2 miles to the SR 153 junction, then SR 153 south about 12 miles to County Road 1029 and on to CR 1034 (Gold Creek Road). CR 1034 becomes Forest Road 4340 after roughly 5 miles; continue about 1.6 miles further on FR 4340, then turn onto FR 4340-300 (Crater Creek Road) and follow it 4.6 miles to the trailhead. An alternate description of the same drive starts from Carlton: south on SR 153 for 3.5 miles, right on Gold Creek Loop Road 1.6 miles, right on Gold Creek Road 5.0 miles (becomes FR 4340), 1.6 miles more, then left on FR 4340-300 for 4.4 miles. The gravel is washboarded in places — drive it slowly. From the trailhead take Eagle Lakes Trail #431. The first 0.7 mile climbs gently, rounds a bend into an opening with a view up the Eagle Creek valley, then descends slightly to the bridge over Crater Creek. From there the trail climbs at a consistently gentle grade through mature pine into subalpine fir and larch. At roughly 5 miles the trail reaches the Eagle Lakes area and forks: take the right fork toward Upper Eagle Lake (7,115 ft, 48.213553 / -120.346815, about 6.2 trail miles and 2,350–2,430 ft of gain from the car). Upper Eagle Lake has many campsites and a large horse camp, and is the last reliable water. From the lake, the East Face of Bigelow is the wall directly above to the northwest — bear northwest up talus and heather to the base of the golden granite, roughly 0.4–0.5 mile and 900–1,000 ft above the lake. The FA party put the whole approach at about 8 miles and ~3,500 ft from the trailhead to the base, on a good, fast trail. Scout the line from the lake and from the base before racking up; the crack systems are genuinely hard to read from below.
descent: There is no rappel descent and no need for one. From the top of pitch 4 you are standing on the summit ridge; coil the ropes, stow the rack, and walk north a short distance to the true 8,449 ft summit. To get down, retrace the standard scramble line: from the summit, drop southeast and then east down the slopes and gullies that stay right (south) of the prominent rock wall you just climbed — do not try to downclimb into the top of the East Face. The scramble down is Class 2 with a couple of Class 3 moves and about 1,330 ft of loss to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,115 ft. Trend toward the lake basin rather than cutting straight down; the terrain immediately below the wall is broken and steep. Once at the lake, rejoin Eagle Lakes Trail #431 and follow it back down past the Eagle Lakes junction, over the Crater Creek bridge, and out to the Crater Creek Trailhead — roughly 6 miles of very good, fast trail. If you are benighted, Upper Eagle Lake has plentiful established campsites and water and is a far better place to sit out the dark than the loose ground under the face. In an early- or late-season attempt with snow on the slopes, the descent to the lake is the crux of the day rather than the climb — carry an axe.
hazards: Rockfall generated by the climbers themselves is the dominant hazard: cracks must be cleaned of sand and brittle flakes before they will take a jam, and the FA party did all of it by hand and boot, showering the belay.
Brittle, lichen-covered holds mean the face climbing is only as solid as your testing discipline — the first-ascensionists broke edges off routinely as they climbed.
The wall is close to vertical for its full 360 ft, so any fall is clean but long, and the pitch-3 traverse crux produces a pendulum.
The approach and descent cross loose talus and heather benches above Upper Eagle Lake, terrain that is slippery when wet and treacherous when snow-covered in early or late season.
This is designated Wilderness roughly six trail miles from the trailhead with no documented cell coverage, so a serious injury means a long, unassisted wait for Okanogan County SAR.
Afternoon convective thunderstorms are a recurring summer pattern on the east slope of the Cascades and there is no shelter anywhere on the face.
Wildfire and smoke are a genuine seasonal hazard in the Sawtooths; the range has closed to entry in past late summers.
